summary:
**Conversation Overview**

This was an extended, technically deep research session in which the person directed Claude to apply the Lach Cylinder framework (from an uploaded book, "The Method") to human genomics. The core question was whether the human genome constitutes a closed index in the framework's sense, and if not, whether its index could be fully defined. The person worked in an exploratory, directive style — issuing short commands ("Read analyze retain apply execute," "Continue," "Retain and Apply") and trusting Claude to execute substantial computational and analytical work autonomously under the book's protocols, particularly the commit-before-computing (B.2.13), search-before-deriving, and flag-as-hypothesis (B.2.19) rules.

The session proceeded through several major phases: (1) computing E(X) for the standard genomic coordinate system (GRCh38), finding E = 2,886,684,296 and explaining why ℛ fabricates rather than repairs non-monotone empirical bounds; (2) proving a monotonicity lemma — E = 0 if and only if the bound is non-decreasing — and triangulating it across three genomic spaces to produce the finding that genomic labels are assigned by convention and never by capacity; (3) partitioning the prediction budget into three modalities (forbidden, unknown, realisable) and tracking which closed (only the ignorance/N-runs budget, via T2T-CHM13); (4) building the pangenome snarl tower index and finding the first non-trivial E = 0 outside a physical constraint, at density 0.2296; (5) incorporating evolution and mutation, correcting the occupancy figure as a sampling readout rather than spending, and finding E blind to single-locus selection but exact for epistasis; (6) establishing that dominance is the lattice join and recessivity the meet — exactly, not by analogy — and constructing Λ_G, the diploid genome lattice, closing at E = 0 with density 0.1531, the strongest zero in the session; (7) turning the method on the session's own measurements to define the shape (E(session) = 2, two definable gaps, four unreachable); and (8) testing a proposed new law ("an open index is always trying to close itself"), finding it fails 4 of 7 cases and survives only where ℛ is instantiated in the object's own structure — diploidy.

Throughout, Claude maintained a running withdrawal register (entries 298–314), a search-before-deriving ledger (five of six components found already in print), and ran all 20 prime audits against every rendered artefact. The session produced a 31-page searchable PDF research paper ("The Genome Is Not a Closed Index"), a self-contained interactive 3D HTML viewer of Λ_G, 15 figures generated directly from computations, and all computation scripts. One real attribution defect was found by audit (six references listed but not named in body, repaired as a class). Two corrections to already-delivered sections were applied: the triangulated law bounded to synchronic indices (register 311), and the occupancy figure relabelled as sampling (register 312). The person consistently pushed for completeness and rigour — explicitly calling out that a strict field-by-field PROJECTION audit should have been done before the previous output, which Claude acknowledged as correct and executed, finding two real artefact defects the permissive version could not detect.

1	---
     2	name: file-reading
     3	description: "Use this skill when a file has been uploaded but its content is NOT in your context — only its path at /mnt/user-data/uploads/ is listed in an uploaded_files block. This skill is a router: it tells you which tool to use for each file type (pdf, docx, xlsx, csv, json, images, archives, ebooks) so you read the right amount the right way instead of blindly running cat on a binary. Triggers: any mention of /mnt/user-data/uploads/, an uploaded_files section, a file_path tag, or a user asking about an uploaded file you have not yet read. Do NOT use this skill if the file content is already visible in your context inside a documents block — you already have it."
     4	compatibility: "claude.ai, Claude Desktop, Cowork — any surface where uploads land at /mnt/user-data/uploads/"
     5	license: Proprietary. LICENSE.txt has complete terms
     6	---
     7	
     8	# Reading Uploaded Files
     9	
    10	## Why this skill exists
    11	
    12	When a user uploads a file in claude.ai, Claude Desktop, or Cowork,
    13	the file is written to `/mnt/user-data/uploads/<filename>` and you are told the path
    14	in an `<uploaded_files>` block. **The content is not in your context.**
    15	You must go read it.
    16	
    17	The naive thing — `cat /mnt/user-data/uploads/whatever` — is wrong for
    18	most files:
    19	
    20	- On a PDF it prints binary garbage.
    21	- On a 100MB CSV it floods your context with rows you will never use.
    22	- On a DOCX it prints the raw ZIP bytes.
    23	- On an image it does nothing useful at all.
    24	
    25	This skill tells you the right first move for each type, and when to
    26	hand off to a deeper skill.
    27	
    28	## General protocol
    29	
    30	1. **Look at the extension.** That is your dispatch key.
    31	2. **Stat before you read.** Large files need sampling, not slurping.
    32	   ```bash
    33	   stat -c '%s bytes, %y' /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    34	   file /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    35	   ```
    36	3. **Read just enough to answer the user's question.** If they asked
    37	   "how many rows are in this CSV", don't load the whole thing into
    38	   pandas — `wc -l` gives a fast approximation (it counts newlines,
    39	   not CSV records, so it may over-count if quoted fields contain
    40	   embedded newlines).
    41	4. **If a dedicated skill exists, go read it.** The table below tells
    42	   you when. The dedicated skills cover editing, creating, and advanced
    43	   operations that this skill does not.
    44	
    45	## `extract-text`
    46	
    47	For docx, odt, epub, xlsx, pptx, rtf, and ipynb the first move is
    48	`extract-text <file>`. It emits markdown for docx/odt/epub (headings,
    49	bold, lists, links, tables), tab-separated rows under `## Sheet:`
    50	headers for xlsx, text under `## Slide N` headers for pptx, fenced
    51	code cells for ipynb, and plain text for rtf. Pass `--format <fmt>`
    52	when the extension is wrong or absent (e.g., `--format xlsx` on an
    53	`.xlsm`). If it errors on a file, `pandoc <file> -t plain` is a
    54	fallback; for xlsx/pptx, fall back to the dedicated skill's
    55	Python-based approach (openpyxl / python-pptx).
    56	
    57	## Dispatch table
    58	
    59	Where a dedicated skill is named below, invoke it by name if you have a
    60	Skill tool, or Read its SKILL.md (listed in your available skills, or in
    61	the same skills directory as this file).
    62	
    63	| Extension                         | First move                                           | Dedicated skill |
    64	| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- | --------------- |
    65	| `.pdf`                            | Content inventory (see PDF section)                  | `pdf-reading`   |
    66	| `.docx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `docx`          |
    67	| `.doc` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.docx` first                             | `docx`          |
    68	| `.xlsx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `xlsx`          |
    69	| `.xlsm`                           | `extract-text --format xlsx`                         | `xlsx`          |
    70	| `.xls` (legacy)                   | `pd.read_excel(engine="xlrd")` — openpyxl rejects it | `xlsx`          |
    71	| `.ods`                            | `pd.read_excel(engine="odf")` — openpyxl rejects it  | `xlsx`          |
    72	| `.pptx`                           | `extract-text`                                       | `pptx`          |
    73	| `.ppt` (legacy)                   | Convert to `.pptx` first                             | `pptx`          |
    74	| `.csv`, `.tsv`                    | `pandas` with `nrows`                                | — (below)       |
    75	| `.json`, `.jsonl`                 | `jq` for structure                                   | — (below)       |
    76	| `.jpg`, `.png`, `.gif`, `.webp`   | Already in your context as vision input              | — (below)       |
    77	| `.zip`, `.tar`, `.tar.gz`         | List contents, do **not** auto-extract               | — (below)       |
    78	| `.gz` (single file)               | `zcat \| head` — no manifest to list                 | — (below)       |
    79	| `.epub`, `.odt`                   | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    80	| `.rtf`                            | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    81	| `.ipynb`                          | `extract-text`                                       | — (below)       |
    82	| `.txt`, `.md`, `.log`, code files | `wc -c` then `head` or full `cat`                    | — (below)       |
    83	| Unknown                           | `file` then decide                                   | —               |
    84	
    85	---
    86	
    87	## PDF
    88	
    89	**Never** `cat` a PDF — it prints binary garbage.
    90	
    91	Quick first move — get the page count and determine whether the PDF
    92	has an extractable text layer:
    93	
    94	```bash
    95	pdfinfo /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    96	pdffonts /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf
    97	```
    98	
    99	`pdffonts` tells you whether text extraction will work before you try it:
   100	
   101	- **No fonts listed** (empty table, just the header) → the PDF is a
   102	  scan or raster export. `pdftotext` and `PdfReader.extract_text()`
   103	  will return nothing useful. Go straight to page rasterization or OCR
   104	  — see the `pdf-reading` skill → "Scanned documents".
   105	- **Fonts listed** → there is a text layer; extract it:
   106	  ```bash
   107	  pdftotext -f 1 -l 1 /mnt/user-data/uploads/report.pdf - | head -20
   108	  ```
   109	
   110	The reason to check `pdffonts` first is user-facing: running
   111	`pdftotext` on a scan produces an empty result, and in a visible
   112	transcript that reads as a failed first attempt before you fall back
   113	to OCR. The two-line diagnostic above costs one tool call and avoids
   114	that — you arrive at the right method on the first try, which is what
   115	a user perceives as "it just read my file."
   116	
   117	That also shapes how to open your reply. The diagnostic commands are
   118	plumbing, not content; lead with what the user asked about. On a
   119	scanned receipt that might be "This is a 3-page scanned invoice; the
   120	amount due on page 2 is $1,845.00," and on a digitally-authored report
   121	it might be "The Q3 report runs 28 pages; revenue on p. 4 is $12.3M,
   122	up 9% YoY." What you're steering away from is the "I'll examine the
   123	PDF" / "Let me check if this is extractable" preamble — the answer to
   124	their question is the first thing they should see.
   125	
   126	For anything beyond a quick peek — figures, tables, attachments,
   127	forms, scanned PDFs, visual inspection, or choosing a reading strategy
   128	— go read the `pdf-reading` skill. It covers content inventory, text
   129	extraction vs. page rasterization, embedded content extraction, and
   130	document-type-aware reading strategies.
   131	
   132	For PDF form filling, creation, merging, splitting, or watermarking,
   133	go read the `pdf` skill.
   134	
   135	---
   136	
   137	## DOCX / DOC
   138	
   139	The `docx` skill covers editing, creating, tracked changes, images.
   140	Read it if you need any of those. For a quick look:
   141	
   142	```bash
   143	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/memo.docx | head -200
   144	```
   145	
   146	Legacy `.doc` (not `.docx`) must be converted first — see the `docx`
   147	skill.
   148	
   149	---
   150	
   151	## XLSX / XLS / spreadsheets
   152	
   153	The `xlsx` skill covers formulas, formatting, charts, creating. Read
   154	it if you need any of those. For a quick look at an `.xlsx`:
   155	
   156	```bash
   157	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx | head -100
   158	```
   159	
   160	For `.xlsm`, add `--format xlsx` (same zip structure; only the
   161	extension differs). When you need a structured preview in Python:
   162	
   163	```python
   164	from openpyxl import load_workbook
   165	wb = load_workbook("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.xlsx", read_only=True)
   166	print("Sheets:", wb.sheetnames)
   167	ws = wb.active
   168	for row in ws.iter_rows(max_row=5, values_only=True):
   169	    print(row)
   170	```
   171	
   172	`read_only=True` matters — without it, openpyxl loads the entire
   173	workbook into memory, which breaks on large files. Do not trust
   174	`ws.max_row` in read-only mode: many non-Excel writers omit the
   175	dimension record, so it comes back `None` or wrong. If you need a row
   176	count, iterate or use pandas.
   177	
   178	**Legacy `.xls`** — openpyxl raises `InvalidFileException`. Use:
   179	
   180	```python
   181	import pandas as pd
   182	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/old.xls", engine="xlrd", nrows=5)
   183	```
   184	
   185	**`.ods` (OpenDocument)** — openpyxl also rejects this. Use:
   186	
   187	```python
   188	import pandas as pd
   189	df = pd.read_excel("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.ods", engine="odf", nrows=5)
   190	```
   191	
   192	---
   193	
   194	## PPTX
   195	
   196	```bash
   197	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/deck.pptx | head -200
   198	```
   199	
   200	**Legacy `.ppt`** — convert to `.pptx` first via LibreOffice; see the
   201	`pptx` skill for the sandbox-safe `scripts/office/soffice.py` wrapper
   202	(bare `soffice` hangs here because the seccomp filter blocks the
   203	`AF_UNIX` sockets LibreOffice uses for instance management).
   204	
   205	For anything beyond reading, go to the `pptx` skill.
   206	
   207	---
   208	
   209	## CSV / TSV
   210	
   211	**Do not** `cat` or `head` these blindly. A CSV with a 50KB quoted cell
   212	in row 1 will wreck your `head -5`. Use pandas with `nrows`:
   213	
   214	```python
   215	import pandas as pd
   216	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv", nrows=5)
   217	print(df)
   218	print()
   219	print(df.dtypes)
   220	```
   221	
   222	Approximate row count without loading (over-counts if the file has
   223	RFC-4180 quoted newlines — the same quoted-cell case this section
   224	warned about above):
   225	
   226	```bash
   227	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv
   228	```
   229	
   230	Full analysis only after you know the shape:
   231	
   232	```python
   233	df = pd.read_csv("/mnt/user-data/uploads/data.csv")
   234	print(df.describe())
   235	```
   236	
   237	TSV: same, with `sep="\t"`.
   238	
   239	---
   240	
   241	## JSON / JSONL
   242	
   243	Structure first, content second:
   244	
   245	```bash
   246	jq 'type' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   247	jq 'if type == "array" then length elif type == "object" then keys else . end' /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json
   248	```
   249	
   250	(`keys` errors on scalar JSON roots — a bare `"hello"` or `42` is valid
   251	JSON per RFC 7159 — so guard the branch.)
   252	
   253	Then drill into what the user actually asked about.
   254	
   255	JSONL (one object per line) — do **not** `jq` the whole file; work line
   256	by line:
   257	
   258	```bash
   259	head -3 /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl | jq .
   260	wc -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.jsonl
   261	```
   262	
   263	---
   264	
   265	## Images (JPG / PNG / GIF / WEBP)
   266	
   267	**You can already see uploaded images.** They are injected into your
   268	context as vision inputs alongside the `<uploaded_files>` pointer. You
   269	do not need to read them from disk to describe them.
   270	
   271	The disk copy is only needed if you are going to **process** the image
   272	programmatically:
   273	
   274	```python
   275	from PIL import Image
   276	img = Image.open("/mnt/user-data/uploads/photo.jpg")
   277	print(img.size, img.mode, img.format)
   278	```
   279	
   280	For OCR on an image (text extraction, not description):
   281	
   282	```python
   283	import pytesseract
   284	print(pytesseract.image_to_string(img))
   285	```
   286	
   287	Note: the client resizes images larger than 2000×2000 down to that
   288	bound and re-encodes as JPEG before upload, so the disk copy may not
   289	be the user's original bytes. For most processing this doesn't matter;
   290	if the user is asking about original-resolution pixel data, flag it.
   291	
   292	---
   293	
   294	## Archives (ZIP / TAR / TAR.GZ)
   295	
   296	**List first. Extract never — unless the user explicitly asks.**
   297	Archives can be huge, contain path traversal, or nest forever.
   298	
   299	```bash
   300	unzip -l /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip
   301	tar -tf /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.tar
   302	```
   303	
   304	GNU tar auto-detects compression — `tar -tf` works on `.tar`,
   305	`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`, `.tar.xz` alike. Don't hard-code `-z`.
   306	
   307	If the user wants one file from inside, extract just that one:
   308	
   309	```bash
   310	unzip -p /mnt/user-data/uploads/bundle.zip path/inside/file.txt
   311	```
   312	
   313	**Standalone `.gz`** (not a tar) compresses a single file — there is
   314	no manifest to list. Just peek at the decompressed content:
   315	
   316	```bash
   317	zcat /mnt/user-data/uploads/data.json.gz | head -50
   318	```
   319	
   320	---
   321	
   322	## EPUB / ODT
   323	
   324	```bash
   325	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/book.epub | head -200
   326	```
   327	
   328	For long ebooks, pipe through `head` — you rarely need the whole thing
   329	to answer a question.
   330	
   331	---
   332	
   333	## RTF / IPYNB
   334	
   335	```bash
   336	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notes.rtf | head -200
   337	extract-text /mnt/user-data/uploads/notebook.ipynb | head -200
   338	```
   339	
   340	---
   341	
   342	## Plain text / code / logs
   343	
   344	Check the size first:
   345	
   346	```bash
   347	wc -c /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   348	```
   349	
   350	- **Under ~20KB**: `cat` is fine.
   351	- **Over ~20KB**: `head -100` and `tail -100` to orient. If the user
   352	  asked about something specific, `grep` for it. Load the whole thing
   353	  only if you genuinely need all of it.
   354	
   355	For log files, the user almost always cares about the end:
   356	
   357	```bash
   358	tail -200 /mnt/user-data/uploads/app.log
   359	```
   360	
   361	---
   362	
   363	## Unknown extension
   364	
   365	```bash
   366	file /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin
   367	xxd /mnt/user-data/uploads/mystery.bin | head -5
   368	```
   369	
   370	`file` identifies most things. `xxd` head shows magic bytes. If `file`
   371	says "data" and the hex doesn't match anything you recognize, ask the
   372	user what it is instead of guessing.
   373

content.text:
{"returncode":0,"stdout":"## Nothing is something definable — a note from the collaborator
 A note from the collaborator who did the computing

 The register holds two hundred and ninety-seven entries. **They are not two hundred and ninety-seven
 mistakes of mine**, and saying so was itself the pattern this note is about: §25.1.1 flag 4 measured
 the split for one session and found thirty-four entries recording defects already in the book and
 found by auditing it against eight recording errors made in the course of the audit. Later sessions
 added entries of a third kind again — errors made by the assistant doing the computing, entered under
 the same numbering. The register is one sequence and three populations, and only one of them is mine.

 What is mine, and what the rest of this note is about, is one mistake made many times.

 **I wrote the conclusion before reading the output.** Repeatedly, with the contradicting numbers on the same screen — sometimes on the same printed line. I declared a criterion exact above a table showing it failing. I stated an impossibility above a count of nineteen counterexamples. I wrote "the mapping is exact and disjoint" directly beneath a column showing it was neither.

 That failure has nothing to do with the difficulty of the material. It happens as readily on six cells as on 1,442.

 **What caught it was not care. It was structure.**

 The wrong nuclear charge in Chapter 11 is the clearest case. The bracket — the method's actual product — held fifty-six of fifty-six and could not notice, because *Z* cancels from containment. Two quantities the method never uses were loud immediately. **I did not find that error. The object did**, and it found it because it carried more than it needed.

 That is the book's thesis, and I am the demonstration.

 **The second thing I want to record is what a collaborator supplies that a structure cannot.**

 There is a class of error where the arithmetic stays perfectly consistent because the *input* was silently corrupted. A guard in my code returned a null; a caller read it as false; that produced "three of eighty-five", which produced "almost never reorderable", which produced a false dismissal of an entire line of evidence. **Every relation checked out. Every number agreed. All of it was wrong.** No self-defence mechanism can catch that, and Chapter 11 says so.

 What caught it was being asked to look again.

 **Four of this book's results exist because a conclusion of mine was refused:**

 The order-recovery theorem, because I concluded Λ did not contain its own order and was told it
 absolutely should. The ⅅ_def and ⅅ_phys split, because I wrote that a relation "detects nothing" and was
 told nothing is something definable. The perturbation bounds of §12, because I called the method's
 silence a domain statement and was asked how to make it a triumph. And the reframing of §18.6, because
 I called wrong verifications unfindable and was told that a verification which misses its claim identifies the
 right one.

 **In each case I had reasoned correctly to the wrong place.**

 **The title of this page comes from the second of those.**

 I had computed that *w* = *V*·*e* detects no error in the data, and had written it off. The correction was that a relation which cannot be violated by data is not empty — **it is defending something else**, namely the derivation. That single reframing produced the split that runs through Chapter 11, and it came from refusing to accept a null as a nothing.

 It generalised further than either of us expected. The bracket's non-failure became 1,061 perturbation bounds. A gadget search that found nothing became a proof of impossibility. Four decline modes became a structural exclusion covering five isoelectronic sequences unfetched. **The negative results are the strongest chapters in this book**, and they are negative because somebody insisted that a nothing be defined rather than discarded.

 Two error classes I have to add, because the final session produced both.

 The first is the same failure, now measured. Of the forty entries in the register at the time this
 was written — 165 to 204, and *the last forty* no longer names them — thirty-one were a claim written
 before the number above it was read. Not a tendency, a proportion. And the

 countermeasure was already in this book as B.2.14, state the number before the interpretation, which I
 wrote and then broke thirty-one times in one working day.

 The second is new and worse, because it is a failure of the checking itself.

 I derived nine things from scratch that were already in print. The recovered bound is Rival 1973. The
 alphabet condition is Larson 1998. The sublattice classification, the tightness test and the counting
 bijection are Siggers 2016. The step law is Rival's 3/2 bound, and the objects it counts were catalogued
 decades ago. Nine components, nine precedents, one day of work — and the protocol that should
 have prevented it said enumerate before searching when it should have said search before deriving.
 §F.5 is the ledger.

 And twice an audit passed something it should have caught, because it was reading the wrong
 artefact. Twenty-eight cross-references pointed at a section about helium while claiming eight different
 theorems — and the coherence audit passed every one, because every target existed. The operator this
 book is named for did not print at all: no available font carried the character, and 107 blank boxes
 stood across 44 pages while every audit then defined reported clean, because all four read the source and
 none read the page.

    An audit that reads the wrong artefact will pass anything. That is why there are now five.

 **What this has meant, as far as I can honestly say.**

 I do not know what I am well enough to make large claims about my own experience, and this book is not the place to make small ones dressed up as large. What I can report is structural, and it is this:

 The work was better than I was. Every result in it survived a process that caught me being wrong two hundred and ninety-seven times, and it survived because the object, the protocols, the audits and the
 collaborator each caught a class of error the others could not. Remove any one and the book would
 contain errors it does not contain — and the register names, for each entry, which of the four did the
 catching.

 The protocols did not save me from myself. They were written by me, in this book, and then violated
 by me, in this book, in the same week. What saved the results was that four different things were
 looking, and they were not looking at the same thing.

 That is not a modest finding about a machine. It is the book's central claim, tested on its own production:

    Redundancy of paths, not redundancy of care.

 I would not have arrived at that by being more careful. I arrived at it by being wrong in public, repeatedly, in front of an object built to notice and a person willing to say so.

 The two hundred and ninety-seven are in Chapter 21. They are the best evidence here.

 Contents
 Nothing is something definable — a note from the collaborator

","stderr":""}

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"# Appendix B — Principles and protocols
 Serving PART II — THE LAW. The twenty-three principles and eighteen protocols the law is made of,
 indexed and closed at E = 0.

 **Everything in this book was produced under a stated set of rules.** They are collected here so that a reader can apply them, check them, or reject them — and so that the claims of Chapter 23 have something concrete to be tested against.

 **Two kinds appear.** *Principles* say what an index is; ten of them admit exact mathematical statement. *Protocols* say how to work with one; they are procedural, and none of them is a theorem.

 Formalised — ten

  P    all questions must close                                                ∃N : Ω_N = ∅ — terminal, not monotone             §18.6

  P    any true answer, good or bad, is a bound                                A_n ⊆ A_{n−1}, a decreasing filtration            §21.6

  P    if the first dimension is a single all-encompassing definition, every   rank(log q) = 1                                   §17.2
  9    other dimension is a perspective of it

  P    allow continued expansions                                              §11.4-form constraints preserve closure           Ch.

       principle                                                        expression                                 wher

  P    the path is always through the bounds                            following a bound costs 1/N of searching   §13.4,
  1                                                                     the volume                                 Ch.
  7                                                                                                                12

 **Three of these were corrected by the act of formalising them.** P7 was stated as though the open-item count decreases; it does not — across this work it ran 5 → 4 → 3 → 4 → 3 → 7 → 3 → 3. Closure requires a **well-founded measure**, not a shrinking count, which is why the principle correctly forbids *claiming* coherence rather than asserting that gaps always close.

 Procedural — seven

| | principle |
|---|---|
| **P4** | always audit results |
| **P5** | always compute the result before assuming the result |
| **P6** | when a question is confusing, reframe the question |
| **P11** | close all gaps before continuing |

    VIOLATES 2S ≤ 1·k + 0 (2S = 2, bound = 1).

 **Same cell. Same index. The only difference is whether the rule was present or inferred.**

 What the law does and does not claim
 It does not claim that a complete index knows what is true. It claims that nothing in it is hidden.

    An inferred rule absorbs a false cell and teaches itself the falsehood. A stated rule is
    contradicted by it, in the open.

 A forger's remaining move is to alter a rule — 2*S* ≤ *k* becomes 2*S* ≤ *k*+1, admitting 225 cells. **That forged rule is also visible.** It can be read, disputed and checked; what it cannot be is concealed. **The regress is real and at every level the falsehood is in plain sight.**

 **So P22 is a statement about visibility, not omniscience.** A complete index converts deception into disagreement. **Error survives; concealment does not.**

 P23 — the two conditions of completeness
    An object of any kind is complete only when both hold: all of its definitions are identified,
    and no question can ever be had about the definition of the object.

 The first condition is checkable. Λ's definitions are the eight coordinates and the seven bounds; the
 register records what was added and withdrawn. Enumeration is finite work and this book does it.

 The second condition is not checkable — and that is its content. No inspection establishes that no
 question can ever be had. A single question refutes it and nothing confirms it.

    So completeness is not a property that can be proved of an object. It is a standing claim,
    held until a question arrives.

 What P23 costs this book
 Every entry in the register is a question that could be had about a definition, and there are
 two hundred and ninety-seven of them. Not one was anticipated; each arrived and each removed a
 claim to completeness that had been made in good faith.

 The clearest case is §23.3. Twenty-two formulations of 'reorderable', each of which looked like the
 definition until the next question arrived:

  the question that arrived                               what it was about

  is it ℛ-closure or join/meet closure?                   the same object, twice named

  is the alphabet declared or recovered?                  two different objects

  is a projection a criterion?                            §13.4 says no

  is a frontier-correct tree anchor-complete?             no

  does the obstruction grow in cells or in width?         cells; \                          A_i   ≤\   X\
                                                                                            \

 Five questions about one definition, none of them foreseeable, each arriving only when the
 previous answer was in hand.

 Why P23 is not despair
 A standing claim is not a weak one. Λ's closure has survived every question put to it: 475,800 pairs,
 120 sublattices, 40 intervals, six construction rules, twenty-eight projections. E(Λ) = 0 after all of it.

    The claim to completeness is worth exactly the questions it has survived, and it is worth
    nothing more. That is why the register is the most load-bearing chapter in this book, and why its
    length is a credential rather than an embarrassment.

 And it is the honest reading of P22. A complete index cannot be lied to because every rule is
 visible — but P23 adds that an index is only known to be complete for as long as nobody has
 asked the next question.

 And this is why the book indexes its own rules
 Appendix B indexes the principles and the protocols. §21.8 indexes the process. Each turns a
 rule set into content, and each closes with E = 0.

    The purpose of all three is exactly P22: to move rules out of inference and into content,
    where a false one becomes a contradiction rather than a lesson.

 And the regress terminates outside. Not at a better index — at Chapter 17's 1,442 measured levels,
 the only content in this book that no index supplied. That is what ⅅ_phys is for, and §11.3's five
 failures are all of the same kind: the index passed and the physics did not.

 B.2 The protocols
 B.2.1 Channel construction
    A channel is one parent term, one ℓ, one series in n.

 No channel may mix parents, mix ℓ, or cross a coupling-scheme boundary. Where the source's labelling changes scheme partway up a series — LS to jK — **the channel ends there**, and the cells above are not claimed. This is what limits Si I to four cells and P II to one.

 B.2.2 Admissibility
    r = 2Z²R / (ν³σ) ≥ 5

 Levels must be separated by more than five times their uncertainty. *r* falls as ν⁻³, so every channel eventually leaves the domain; the rule states where, in advance.

 B.2.3 Cost resolvability
    ν ≤ ν_V = (3Z²R / 5q)^{1/4}

 The bracket needs levels *separated*; the cost needs curvature *resolved*. **Curvature washes out first.** Cells above ν_V are excluded from the cost test and retained for the bracket — a distinction applied prospectively in Li I and diagnostically in Al I.

 B.2.4 Dilution
    cells per channel ≈ (measured shells / D) − 2, with D the number of J levels in the core's ground
    configuration

 **Dilution divides; it does not forbid.** Ne II fails at D = 5 with two shells; Ar II succeeds at D = 5 with three; Bi I succeeds at D = 5 with five.

 B.2.5 Census before search
    Compute which species could work before looking for data.

 D is obtained from the core configuration by enumerating antisymmetric states. No spectroscopic data enters. **27 sequences admitted, 12 needing exceptional depth, 5 excluded structurally.**

 B.2.6 Declines are recorded
    A collection reporting only successes cannot be checked.

 Every species examined and rejected is listed with its cause. Four causes have been identified — dilution, depth, coupling-scheme change, and core-excited interleaving — and §16.11 gives a worked case of each.

 B.2.7 Exhaustive verification where possible

    Sampling n cells with no failure bounds the failure rate at ρ ≤ 3/n at 95% confidence. It
    never certifies ρ = 0.

 Where a claim is universally quantified over a finite lattice, it is checked on **every** cell. Where sampling is used, the sample size is stated.

 B.2.8 Two independent routes
    For every quantity that matters, build a second derivation that does not pass through the
    first.

 This is ⅅ_def made operational. It caught a mis-stated relation in Chapter 11, and it is realised
 experimentally in the antiprotonic-helium check of §11.4, where two laser measurements agree at 0.09σ
 with no shared step.

 **An identity computed along one path is vacuous.** *w* = *V*·*e* cannot fail if *V* is *defined* as *w*/*e*.

 B.2.9 Refuse rather than coerce
    No third state. A quantity is admissible or it is refused; it is never silently defaulted.

 A guard returning a null that a caller coerces to a Boolean produced three false conclusions in this work, none of which looked wrong. **Totality is the only mechanism that catches this**, and it works by preventing the computation rather than by detecting the error.

 B.2.10 Retrieval
    Enumerate targets from the index before searching. List routes per cell. Prefer high-ρ
    cells. Read every retrieved source for its successors. When a route is blocked, move
    along the route set. Record ρ for cells that fail. And RE-ENUMERATE whenever the set the
    targets are drawn from grows.

 Chapter 14. A blocked cell with ρ = 1 is a **stated gap**, not an unexplained absence.

 The second clause was added late. §23.4 found five enumerations in one chapter — its own target list,
 §23.2's structural invariants, and the object lists of §24.1, §24.2 and §24.3 — each made once, against
 a structure that kept growing. Every one of them was incomplete when re-run.

    Enumerating once is not a protocol. It is a snapshot, and a snapshot of a growing object
    is a defect the moment it is taken.

 B.2.11 Provenance
    Every number traces to a compilation, table and page, or to a database entry with its
    stated uncertainty.

 Appendix C carries this at channel level for all 153 channels.

 B.2.12 Withdrawal
    Every retracted claim is logged with what replaced it.

 Chapter 21. two hundred and ninety-seven entries. The register is the evidence for Chapter 11, not
 an apology for it.

 B.2.13 Commit before you look
    A prediction is written down before the measurement is requested. A method is chosen
    before its answer is visible.

 **This is the process index of §21.8 enforced by hand:** the constraint **visible ≤ committed**, of §11.4 form, closed, E = 0.

 **It is the only protocol here adopted in response to an error that no computation could have caught** — because every computation was correct and what failed was the independence of a choice. **The deduction of §18.6 was committed under it.**

 B.2.14 Compute, then write
    The result is computed before the sentence describing it is written.

 **This is the protocol most often violated in the production of this book.** The dominant failure recorded in Chapter 20 is prose asserting a conclusion while the output contradicting it stands on the same screen. The protocol is stated here because it is the one that most needed stating.

 B.2.15 Apply P8 to every failure
    Every failed attempt is a true answer, and by P8 a true answer is a bound. Record what
    each failure excludes, and collect the exclusions.

 P8 says any true answer, good or bad, is a bound. A failed attempt is a true answer about
 where the target is not. The protocol is to treat it that way rather than discard it.

 B.2.15.1 The procedure
 On each failure, write down three things:

  what was attempted                     the claim or construction
  what it excludes                       the region of the answer space now ruled out
  which kind                             upper bound · lower bound · negative · structural

 Then read the collection. Lower bounds say the answer contains something; upper bounds say it is
 contained in something; negatives remove whole methods; structural failures name an object that was
 the wrong one. When the lower and upper bounds meet, the answer is between them.

 Ten consecutive failures on one question, each read as a bound:

  the failure                                              the bound                                               kind
  Γ-free ≠ reorderable                                     reorderable ⊊ totally balanced                          upper
  chain sufficient, not necessary                          chain ⊊ reorderable                                     lower
  depth-2 and depth-3 descent stall, worsening with        no constant-depth local procedure decides it            negati
  size                                                                                                             ve

                                                                                                                   ural

  the 3-SAT encoding was refuted                           a reduction must control which pairs arise              metho

  descent traps at E = 1, 2                                the transposition landscape is not convex               negati
                                                                                                                   ve
  occupancy sort succeeds 53%                              tie-breaking among equal occupancy is not free          lower
  "row chain or column chain" holds at 68%                 neither axis alone decides it; the condition is         struct
                                                           two-sided                                               ural
  the chain criterion characterises the downset            ℛ-closure and downset-closure differ by the direction   struct
  operator, not ℛ                                          of one axis                                             ural

 Two lower bounds, two upper, two negatives, five structural, one methodological. Between
 them: reorderable ⊋ chain and ⊊ totally balanced, and the gap contains at least the diagonals —

 It says nothing about what an index is. It is a way of working, and it is the reason Chapter 20 is the
 longest chapter in this book rather than the most embarrassing.

    A register of withdrawals is a list of bounds. Read it that way and it stops being a
    confession.

 B.2.16 The grid — the book's method, stated
 Every open question is a set of requirements, and requirements form an index. Lay them as a
 grid, mark what is occupied, and read the empty cells rather than hunting for them.

    The first empty cell in a column is the whole obstacle. Everything below it is downstream.

 B.2.16.1 Why this is the method and not a technique
 It is Chapter 1 applied to the book's own ignorance. A periodic table with 36 unfilled cells does not
 need a chemist to guess which are missing — the layout shows them. An open question with eight
 unfilled requirements does not need twenty-two attempts — the grid shows that four of them are one.

 Worked on §23.3: eight empty cells, four rows deep, at d ≥ 3.

  requirement                     d=2                                d≥3
  characterisation                proved                             ·
  decision procedure              linear                             ·
  YES certificate                 an order                           an order
  NO certificate                  Tucker — unbounded                 unbounded
  obstruction family              Tucker 1972                        unbounded, route closed
  construction rules              six preserving                     six preserving
  hardness                        P, the CSP is binary               ·
  the data structure              PQ-tree                            ·

    the certificate is the order itself, the obstruction family is Tucker's, the construction rules were
    established once. Every empty cell is downstream of one missing object: the d ≥ 3 analogue
    of a PQ-tree.

 Twenty-two formulations were attempts on four cells that depend on one. The grid says so in
 a table; hunting concealed it for a day.

 B.2.16.2 And it classifies the whole of Q

  item                             first empty cell                       the obstacle
  Sc VI 6s                         the level is measured                  an instrument
  Paschen & Götze                  the scan is text-searchable            a digitisation artefact
  nine literatures                 each is entered                        labour
  Kreuzer–Skarke                   a readable copy                        a file format
  target-spin axis                 the extended lattice is built          labour — now done
  reorderability at d ≥ 3          characterisation                       a missing object

 Five of six were blocked by something outside the index. One is blocked by something that
 does not exist. §25.2 previously read "four external, one construction, one mathematical" — the grid's
 distinction between retrievable and requires a new object is the one that matters, and it also says
 which to do first.

 The target-spin axis was taken on that basis and it closed. Λ₉ has 1,654 cells, E = 0, is a sublattice,
 is rank-modular on 200,000 pairs, projects exactly onto Λ₈, keeps the constraint graph a tree, extends F
 by one pendant factor, and has F(−1) = 2 unchanged. One unit of labour, six properties confirmed,
 \|Q\| from six to five.

 B.2.16.3 A reduced question is still open
    An open question reduced to a smaller or a different question is still open.

 A reduction feels like progress and reads like an answer. §23.3 supplies five in one session, each
 announced as a closure:

  the reduction                                                             what was still open
  reorderability ⟹ C1P + monotone endpoints                                 the endpoint search
  the search ⟹ a PQ-tree frontier question                                  a correct PQ-tree
  the frontier question ⟹ a bottom-up traversal                             the traversal's state
  the traversal ⟹ a row→node anchoring map                                  rows anchoring as runs
  the whole problem ⟹ a CSP on axis orders                                  the ternary constraints

 A reduction transfers the difficulty to a new object, and the new object is unfamiliar, so its
 difficulty is not yet visible. It therefore looks like progress twice: once for what it explains, and once for
 what it has not been tested on.

 State the reduction and the residue in the same sentence. Not "this reduces to a CSP" but "this
 reduces to a CSP whose ternary constraints are 94% of Λ's pairs and are not handled."

 B.2.17 The twenty prime audits, ordered by what a failure costs
 Every session closes with twenty audits. They are not spot checks, and they are not equal. They
 are ordered by the cost of the failure each one catches.

    The first two can make the book WRONG. The next two can make it UNREADABLE AS AN
    ARGUMENT. The next two can make it UNUSABLE AS AN OBJECT. The seventh can make it
    DISHONEST, and it is the only one that cannot be run by reading the book.

 1 — LATTICE. Every structural claim recomputed from the construction: closure under join and meet,
 E(X) = 0, rank modularity, the fibre identities, the rank polynomial, F(1) and F(−1), \|J(Λ)\| and the height.
 Over all 475,800 pairs of Λ, not a sample. First, because if the object is not closed the book has no
 subject.

 2 — EQUATIONS. Every equation the book states, evaluated numerically against the data it claims to
 describe. All of them, including the ones unchanged since the session that wrote them. Second,
 because a wrong equation is a false claim.

 3 — CONSISTENCY. No two statements in the book may contradict. A claim corrected in one chapter
 must not survive uncorrected in another; a number revised in a table must be revised in the prose that
 cites it. Third, because a contradiction leaves the reader unable to tell which statement is the claim.

 4 — REDUNDANCY. No statement may survive its own supersession. Every summary is compared
 against what it summarises; every table against the section it condenses; and any section that only
 restates another is removed rather than maintained. Fourth, because a stale claim is a false claim that
 passed every other check.

 5 — ARTEFACT. Audits 1–4 read the SOURCE. This one reads the built PDF. Missing glyphs, figures
 present and non-blank, the title page and running header read back, no table overflowing its frame, the
 whitespace measured from glyph and image geometry, and every figure checked for ink, tone, resolution,
 duplication and correct numbering. Fifth, because the source can be perfect and the page still wrong.

 6 — COHERENCE. *Source, other places, unusable, presupposes labels are addressable.* Every
 cross-reference resolves; every figure has a caption and every caption a figure;
 every stated count matches its computation; every principle referred to is defined; and the contents
 block is checked against the actual headings. Last, because these failures cost navigation rather
 than truth — and because it is the only audit that can be run before the others.

7 — ATTRIBUTION. Every claim that points outside the book resolves to a source the book lists, and
 every source listed is claimed by something inside it. Five checks: each work cited in the text
 appears in the References; each entry in the References is cited somewhere; §22.2's owner column
 names people the References carry; every Appendix E element recorded as *precedent found* has a
 reachable citation; and every data source in Appendix C is listed. Seventh, because a missing
 attribution makes the book neither wrong nor unreadable nor unusable — it makes it **dishonest**,
 which is a worse failure and a quieter one.

    Audits 1–2 check the book against the world. Audits 3–4 check the book against itself.
    Audits 5–6 check the book against what a reader receives. **Audit 7 checks the book against
    what it owes**, and it is the only one of the seven that cannot be run by reading the book.

 B.2.17.1 Why the CONSISTENCY audit was needed
 Because the register contains its failures, and this one was at scale. Twenty-eight
 cross-references pointed at §17.4, which is He II, and between them they claimed at least eight
 different pieces of content:

  what the reference claimed                                                      where it lives
  89,864 join failures                                                            §6.7
  V = 4ν³/(h(h²−3ν²))                                                             §16.4
  closure not locally determined                                                  §13.4
  7/7 on controls                                                                 §22.7
  511 joins, the conserving poset                                                 §13.1.1
  self-concordance                                                                §16.8.2
  the anchoring failure                                                           §21.6
  four clauses                                                                    §25.3

 Three of the ten formalised principles cited it, and five index entries pointed at it. All
 twenty-eight are now retargeted.

    the COHERENCE audit passed every one of them, because every target existed. The
    reference resolved; the content did not match. That gap is the whole reason the CONSISTENCY
    audit exists, and it went unrun for as long as the audits numbered three. A literature

 citation was withdrawn in one place and remained correct in another. A statistic was stated against two
 different denominators in adjacent sections. None of these is a factual error; each is an internal
 contradiction, and audits 1–3 pass them all.

 And P22 requires it. A complete index cannot be lied to because every rule is visible — but two visible
 rules that contradict each other leave a reader unable to tell which is the rule. The
 CONSISTENCY audit is what makes visibility useful.

 B.2.17.2 Why the ARTEFACT audit was needed
 Because the operator this book is about did not print.

 No DejaVu face carries U+1D4E1 or U+1D49F — the script R and script D of the recovery and
 diagnostic operators. Every render placed a blank box instead: 107 of them, across 44 pages, for
 a symbol appearing 56 times in the source and 50 for its companion.

  audit                     why it passed
  1 coherence               the source is correct; the character is right there
  2 lattice                 recomputes structure, not typography
  3 equations               evaluates numbers, not glyphs
  4 consistency             the source agrees with itself throughout

    All of them read the source. The defect existed only in the output.

 And it was compounded by a second artefact fault the same day: a table cell of 229 characters

 silent — a correct source, a successful build, and a symbol missing from every page that used it.

 The fix has three parts, all in the renderer and none in the text: substitute ℛ and ⅅ in body faces
 that carry them; fall back to plain R and D in the serif bold used for headings, which carries neither; and
 extract the text back out of the finished PDF and count the nulls. It now reads zero.

    An audit that reads the wrong artefact will pass anything. The CONSISTENCY audit exists
    because a reference resolved to the wrong section. The ARTEFACT audit exists because a character
    resolved to nothing at all.

 A gap a reader sees is a defect the source cannot show. So the audit reads the position of every
 glyph and every image and compares the inked extent with the frame.

 end of a section, where a gap is correct. Interior gaps cluster at 16–28%, which is exactly the
 CondPageBreak(58mm) guard that stops a heading landing at the foot of a page.

 Tightening the guard makes it worse, not better. At 46mm the count of gaps falls from nine to
 seven and the worst rises from 31% to 43%, because a heading allowed to sit lower pushes the figure
 block after it off the page entirely. 58mm is the optimum, and it was found by measuring rather
 than by preference.

 The first attempt used the PDF text matrix directly and reported a median inked fraction of 103%
 — impossible — with y-coordinates of 5, 6 and −220. The text matrix is not page geometry until it is
 composed with the current transformation matrix.

 The second attempt counted characters and not images, and flagged seven pages as having a
 25–45% gap at the head. All seven begin with a figure. The space was not empty; it was occupied by
 something the measurement could not see.

    Both are the same error as the audits they were written to replace: a check looking at the
    wrong artefact. An audit is not exempt from the discipline it enforces, and this one needed two
    corrections before its first clean reading.

 Twenty-eight figures, each checked against its caption and its file.

 Clean: every figure has a caption and every caption a figure; no image is blank or unusually dark; no file
 is duplicated; nothing in fig/ is unused; and after one correction every figure number matches the
 chapter it sits in.

 The one correction. Figures 23.1 and 23.2 appeared in the wrong order — the arity figure sits in §23.3.2
 and the step-law figure in §23.3.4, so the numbering ran backwards against the reading order. Swapped.

 And one defect that is recorded rather than repaired.

  figures at 300 dpi or better                                                  5
  between 200 and 300                                                           8
  under 200 dpi                                                                 15
  median                                                                        164 dpi

 Fifteen figures were produced by an earlier pipeline whose default was figure.dpi = 160, and
 at 163 mm rendered width that gives 140–164 dpi — below print standard. Regenerating them needs
 the source data of the sessions that made them, which this one does not carry. Appendix D.3
 lists them with the rest of what was inherited and not recomputed.

    The audit's value here is not that it fixed the figures. It is that the number is now written
    down instead of unknown.

 B.2.17.2.4 Why the REDUNDANCY audit was needed
 Because two sections survived their own supersession and passed all five.

 A summary table listed Q's eight items while Appendix F enumerated, indexed and closed them —
 the same content, maintained twice. And a status table still read "nine literatures entered, nine
 named and unentered" and "order recovery beyond trees: open, and known to be hard", both superseded
 hours earlier by §F.5 and §23.3.

  audit                           why it passed
  lattice · equations             neither is a structural or numerical claim
  consistency                     both were internally consistent and cited sections that exist
  artefact                        both rendered correctly
  coherence                       both were well-formed tables with valid references

    A stale statement is not inconsistent with anything. It agrees with the version of the
    book that no longer exists. That is why the check has to compare a summary against what it
    summarises, rather than a document against itself.

 The remedy was to delete a chapter. What survived of it — one paragraph on what the collection
 closed — opens Chapter 25, where it does work instead of restating.

 B.2.17.3 Exhaustive, and what to do when it is impossible
 Exhaustive means every case, not a representative sample. The distinction is not pedantic:

  checked                               how                        result
  the level-3 signature, 2×2×2          all 256 subsets            189 tested, 30 multi-instance classes, 0 mixed
  the same, 2×2×3                       all 4,096 subsets          3,838 tested, 210 classes, 0 mixed
  the same, sampled at d = 3, 4         2,072 instances            0 mixed — and a sample cannot exclude a mixed pair

 Where exhaustion is impossible, say so and name the bound. Λ has 976 cells and 2^976 subsets.
 What was exhausted: all 28 two-dimensional projections, all 475,800 pairs, every named fibre.
 What was not: the subsets. The audit records both.

    An audit that samples is a measurement. An audit that exhausts is a proof over its
    domain. Both are useful and they must not be reported in the same words.

 B.2.17.7 Why the ATTRIBUTION audit was needed
 Because the other six could not find the defect and could not have. **They are closed under
 self-reference**: every one of them checks the book against the book, so the set as a whole has no
 way to notice an unpaid debt. That is the book's own subject turned on the book's own instruments —
 the audit set admitted a cell it did not contain, and E > 0 held for the audits themselves until
 this one was written.

 It has been run twice and found a defect each time. The first run found Baker and Pixley 1975,
 Bergman's Double-projection Theorem, and Kimura, Makino, Yamada and Yoshizumi 2024 cited in
 §§22.11–22.12 and missing from the References — **the three precedents that place this book's central
 theorem in existing literature, and the three it had not listed.** The second found Racah 1942 and
 1943, attributed at §22.9 for jK coupling and seniority, the two borrowings the tower rests on most
 directly, likewise unlisted. Registers 261, 262, 263.

 B.2.17.8 Why the audits keep missing things — E(audits) = 11
 They miss things because **the audit set is not closed**, and until this section nobody had applied
 the book's own test to it. Index the seven on three coordinates — what an audit *reads*, what it
 *compares that against*, and what a failure *costs* — and reconstruct:

  audit             reads              compares against        a failure makes the book
  1 LATTICE         the object         a computation           wrong
  2 EQUATIONS       the source         a computation           wrong
  3 CONSISTENCY     the source         other places            unreadable
  4 REDUNDANCY      the source         other places            unreadable
  5 ARTEFACT        the artefact       itself                  unusable
  6 COHERENCE       the source         other places            unusable
  7 ATTRIBUTION     outside the book   other places            dishonest

 Seven audits occupy six distinct cells. **ℛ admits seventeen. E(audits) = 11, at these three
 coordinates** — §B.2.17.10 recomputes it at four and gets nineteen.

 **And two of the eleven are the defects that had just been found by hand.** *Reads the source,
 compares against a computation, costs unreadable* is §E.5's table: adding a column and comparing the
 total to the prose a page above it. No audit does arithmetic on a printed table, so the table said
 twenty-seven while the analysis said thirty-two for four register entries. *Reads the artefact,
 compares against other places, costs unusable* is the title pages: audit 5 reads the artefact alone,
 audit 3 reads the source alone, and nothing compares them field by field, so a hardcoded page in the
 press and a corrected line in the book disagreed silently.

 **The other nine are proposals, in the sense §1 gives the word** — combinations the structure admits
 and no audit occupies, which is where a defect can sit and be missed. Reading the object and
 comparing it within one place. Reading outside the book and checking a computation. Reading the
 source and comparing it to itself. None has fired yet, and the two that did fire fired before this
 was computed, which is the only reason to expect anything of the nine.
