 carried. Both are restated here at twenty, because a hierarchy fixed on a third of a set is a claim
 that expires.

 **The precedences, nineteen of them.** CELL before LATTICE, because a set containing an invalid cell
 has no closure worth testing. LATTICE before EQUATIONS. EQUATIONS before SCOPE, AGREEMENT, ARITHMETIC
 and ENUMERATION, because a property of a number presupposes the number. CONSISTENCY before
 REDUNDANCY; both before ARTEFACT. MARKUP before ARTEFACT and FIDELITY. ARTEFACT before MEASURE,
 FIDELITY and PROJECTION. ATTRIBUTION before REPRODUCTION. **SEQUENCE before ANTECEDENT, COHERENCE
 and PROJECTION** — the newest and the earliest, because a label that is not addressable is invisible
 to every check that consumes labels.

 **Two of the nineteen were unexplained, and the resolution was not a fifth coordinate.** SEQUENCE
 stood before ANTECEDENT and COHERENCE with no coordinate rising between them. §12's loop asks first
 whether an existing coordinate was misread, and it was: ANTECEDENT and COHERENCE were recorded as
 presupposing **nothing**, and they presuppose that labels are addressable — which is what SEQUENCE
 establishes. Both move to *presupposes the claims are individually true*, and **all nineteen
 precedences are then explained by the four coordinates**. No axis was added, which is the outcome
 §12 prefers and the one this book has twice failed to reach for on the first attempt.

 **The measurements, at twenty.** Twenty audits over twenty distinct cells, no collision. The
 precedence order falls into three components of ten, eight and two; the largest has 4,140 linear
 extensions and two of them intersect exactly to the order, so **dim(hierarchy) = 2**, unchanged from
 seven audits to twenty. **E(audits) = 17 at four coordinates**, down from nineteen as SEQUENCE and
 PROJECTION took two of the missing cells.

 **That the dimension held while the set nearly tripled is the finding.** Order dimension measures how
 much *branching* a hierarchy has, not how much of it there is; the audits grew in width and not in
 entanglement. Two coordinates still recover which audit runs before which. The other two still carry
 what an audit *is*, and that division — §B.2.17.11's — is what the growth tested and did not break.
 Register 295.

 B.2.18 Triangulation — three results locate a fourth
    For every three results or bounds that measure the same object, triangulate: they
    identify a related data point that none of them states.

 Three measurements of one thing are not three facts. They are a position.

 B.2.18.1 Worked, from §23.3

  the three                              what they                  the fourth, located
                                         measured
  valid orders disconnected ·            connectivity failure in    the disconnection is in the object, not the space —
  E-landscape traps · cell-growth        three different spaces     so no local method in any space can be complete
  peaks
  step 1 at d = 2 · step 2 at d = 3 ·    growth step, three         step = 2^(d−2), then proved by subcube removal
  step 4 at d = 4                        dimensions
  arity 2 bijunctive · arity 3           the constraint             the boundary is arity 3 and it is exact — the
  bijunctive · arity 4 contains          language                   procedure and the hardness proof are one law read at two
  1-in-3-SAT                                                        arities
  three reductions, all                  the encoding               the map X → C(X) is global, non-separable and
  over-constraining                                                 non-monotone — it admits no local editing

 Each fourth point was invisible in any single measurement and forced by the three together.
 The step law is the clearest: 1, 2, 4 fixed the ¾ ratio, and the ratio gave the subcube construction, which
 proved it.

 B.2.18.2 And it is a check as well as a method
 Triangulation fails loudly. If three measurements of one object do not locate a consistent fourth, one of
 them is wrong — and that is how three corrections were caught in a single session:

 A map that is global, non-separable and non-monotone should have a SMALL image.
 Measured: 39% at d = 3 and 49.5% at d = 4, rising. The three coordinates were right and the
 inference from them was not — they locate an obstruction to EDITING the map, not to its range.

    Three consistent measurements give a fourth result. Three measurements that give no
    consistent fourth give a correction instead. Both outcomes are useful and the protocol does not
    distinguish them in advance.

 B.2.18.3 Why it belongs with the protocols
 It is P8 with a count attached. Every failure is a bound; three bounds on one object are a
 coordinate. B.2.15 says to record failures as bounds; this says what to do once three of them are in
 hand.

 And it composes with B.2.16. The grid shows which cells are empty; triangulation fills one from three
 of its neighbours.


 B.2.19 The seven failures of the assistant, and the protocol each one earns
 Two hundred and ninety-seven entries stand in the register and they are not one population. §25.1.1
 flag 4 separates them: defects already in the book and found by auditing it, errors the author made,
 and errors made by the assistant doing the computing. This section is the third population, sorted
 not by entry but by **kind**, because fourteen entries collapse to seven mechanisms and a mechanism
 is what a protocol can address. Each is stated as the failure, then the rule that would have caught
 it, then the entries that are instances.

 B.2.19.1 Attribute Inward First
 *When a recomputation disagrees with the book, the model is
 the suspect until it is cleared.* Three times a recomputation failed and the shortfall was written
 down as the book's: the density column was called underspecified when the exact sets in my model were
 loose; the thirty-two-against-twenty-seven count was called unsettleable when the arithmetic was on
 the page; the book was said to face an exposure the preface answers in its third paragraph. **The
 rule is asymmetric on purpose** — the book has been audited and the model has not, so the prior
 belongs with the book. Registers 207, 213, 220.

 B.2.19.2 Read The Structure At The Point Of Insertion
 *Before writing into a numbered
 sequence, enumerate what already occupies it.* Four ledger rows were written into Appendix A as
 A.8–A.11 over proofs that already stood there; a heading was written with a leading space into a
 file where that makes it invisible; a contents block was restructured without checking what it
 indexed. Every one is the same act — writing into a structure without reading the structure.
 Registers 215, 218, 259.

 B.2.19.3 A Claim Of Completion Is Itself A Claim
 *Any sentence asserting that work was done
 must be verified by the check it claims to have passed, in the same pass that writes it.* §25.1.2
 stated three things as done that were not done when the section claiming them was built. Three Q
 items were described as *entered in Q* in the sections that named them and never reached Appendix F.
 The failure is not forgetting; it is that describing and doing feel identical while writing.
 Registers 239, 256.

 B.2.19.4 Repair The Class Or Say You Did Not
 *A fix that leaves the mechanism unchanged is an
 instance fix, and must be recorded as one.* An indented heading was repaired in two sections and
 reintroduced in the next turn, because nothing in the press rejected one. Emphasis straddling a cell
 was corrected in the source and recurred at a line boundary, because the parser still worked per
 line. Both are now gates in the press. **The instance is cheap and the class is the work**, and the
 register is the place to say which was done. Registers 259, 260, 264.

 B.2.19.5 A Null Is A Result With Its Definition Missing
 *Before recording that something was
 not found, define what was looked for and count what could have been.* A tripwire run was filed as a
 null at ten checks; defining the implicit-parent case raised it to fifty-four and turned the result
 into two — a specificity measure and a ceiling on published notation. **This is the book's own title
 page** and it took being told. Registers 253, 254.

 B.2.19.6 Show The Test Can Fail
 *A check must be demonstrated capable of returning a failure
 before its passing is evidence of anything.* A character class matched no superscripts and returned
 zero rows as though clean; a summary line was printed by a script that hard-coded it one line below
 the computation refuting it; a lemma looked refuted on 1,098 cases because *strictly* had been
 dropped from the definition. **A test that cannot fail returns no failures**, and that is
 indistinguishable from success until someone checks the checker. Register 227.

 B.2.19.7 A Flag Is A Hypothesis
 *Localise a detector's output before recording it as a
 defect.* A phrase quoted inside a register entry read as a surviving error; a section title beginning
 with a lowercase Greek letter read as a missing proof; a line break inside a bold span read as an
 unprinted claim. Each would have entered the register as the book's failure had it been believed.
 **The audits generate hypotheses, and the register takes only what survives testing.**

 **What the seven have in common, and it is one thing.** Every one is a claim made faster than it was
 checked — outward before inward, into a structure before reading it, of completion before completing,
 of a class from an instance, of a null from an undefined absence, of a pass from an untested test, of
 a defect from an untested flag. **B.2.14 already says it: compute, then write.** These seven are that
 protocol failing in seven distinguishable places, and the reason they are listed separately is that
 knowing the general rule demonstrably did not prevent any of them. Register 266.

 B.2.20 What is computable, and what is decided
 §B.2.17.11 ends by saying a coordinate system answers to two masters and only one of them is
 computable. The word is doing real work and the book has not defined it. It defines it with its own
 operator.

    **A quantity is COMPUTABLE in this book when it is recoverable by ℛ from what the book
    prints** — when two readers running the stated procedure on the printed text return the same
    value, and neither has to decide anything to get there.

 That is not a claim about difficulty. E(Λ) = 0 over 475,800 pairs is computable and took minutes;
 whether A.5's language is order or analysis is not computable and took one sentence.

 **Nineteen quantities in the work of these sessions are computable.** E(Λ) = 0; |J(Λ)| = 17 with its
 twenty covering relations; the Birkhoff down-set count of 976; the alphabet's size Σ(|Aᵢ| − 1) = 17;
 the seventeen-bit encoding with join as OR and meet as AND; the 7.07 bits of surplus; the twenty
 implications cutting 131,072 words to 976; every tower cell count and every density; closure through
 the f shell at 499,246 cells and exhaustively to 47,775,744 ambient ones; the E1 puncture at four
 meets all producing (0,0); the triangle at four caps; lemma 4 over 2,354 interval sets; E(audits) at
 11, 0 and 19; dim(audit hierarchy) = 2; E(G) = 33; E(Q); the tripwire's 150 of 216; the fifty-four
 of one hundred and two. **Each is a function of the printed object and of nothing else.**

 **Ten are decisions, and they are of three kinds.**

 *Frames.* The fibration of Appendix E, the coordinate list for the audits, the caps of §2.4. E is
 computable **given** them and none of them is computed — register 275 is the general statement, that
 a zero is worth the size of the box it was computed in, and the box is chosen.

 *Readings.* Applying a stated criterion to a case it does not settle: whether A.5's proof makes it
 order or analysis, whether the five results are elements under §E.5.3, whether *law* means
 holds-of-every-index or holds-and-forbids. The criterion is printed; the application is a judgement,
 and §E.5.4 marks the one place this work made one and says so.

 *Claims about the outside.* Precedent, novelty, whether a measurement exists. §22.1 proves the first
 of these permanently undecidable in one direction, which is the strongest statement of this kind the
 book contains.

 **And the distinction has a use, not merely a name.** Every computable quantity in this book can be
 checked by a reader with the printed text and no access to its author. Every decision must be
 *stated* rather than checked, and the register is what stating them costs. **The seven prime audits
 of §B.2.17.1–7 test computable claims; nothing tests a decision**, which is why the seventeenth
 through twentieth entries of the register are corrections of computation and the twentieth through
 fortieth are reversals of judgement. The book cannot make its decisions checkable. It can make them
 visible, and that is the whole of what the register is for. Register 277.

 B.2.20.1 The lattice applied to what it cannot compute
 §B.2.20 separates nineteen computed quantities from ten decisions and stops there, on the ground
 that nothing tests a decision. **The shape still applies to them, and it says two things.**

 **First: index the decisions and E finds one that has not been made.** Coordinates *scope*, *how it
 is stated* and *reversibility*, fibred by kind — frame, reading, outside claim. Ten decisions,
 E = 1 fibred and 5 unfibred, with a single cell admitted and absent in the *reading* fibre:

    a reading, scoped to one appendix, stated, freely reversible.

 That cell has an occupant the book declined to seat. Register 270 records that Appendices C and G
 are cited from the body only as wholes and never at section level, calls it a navigability defect,
 and leaves the choice open. **It is a reading, it is confined to two appendices, it is stated, and it
 costs nothing to reverse.** E over the decisions located a deferred decision exactly as E over Q
 located item H — which is the first evidence that the operator has any purchase outside the
 computable.

 **Second, and this is the finding: the decisions form a DAG, and two of them have two parents.**
 The order is acyclic, so the decisions can be made in some sequence and none presupposes itself. Six
 of the ten depend on nothing. But two do not have a single parent:

    the fibration of Appendix E — settled only with the caps of §2.4 **and** what counts as an
    element both in view

    not promoting the six theorems — settled only with the meaning of *law* **and** the audit
    coordinate list both in view

 **This is §7.11's dichotomy, arriving in the one place the book had assumed it did not reach.** A
 single-parent constraint propagates down a tree and is carried exactly; a two-parent constraint
 breaks the tree and admits only an envelope. The tight K has two parents and costs the cylinder
 2,475 cells. A two-parent *decision* is the same shape: **no earlier choice determines it, and it
 cannot be delegated to one predecessor or deferred until one is settled.** It must be made with both
 in view or not at all.

 The book has two such decisions and it stumbled on both. Registers 219 to 222 hold three successive
 positions on the element count, which is the fibration decision made once with the caps in view and
 once with the element criterion in view and never with both. Register 232 declines the promotion and
 says the reason is a trade between two things at once. **Two instances is not a law**, and the
 correspondence is offered as what it is — a shape that fits twice, in a set of ten, where the
 prediction it makes is that any third two-parent decision will be hard in the same way. Register 278.

 B.2.21 What a safe repair requires
 §B.2.17.12 recorded a defect and declined to repair it on the ground that the repair was riskier
 than the defect. That judgement was made without a standard, and this states one.

    A repair is **safe** when five conditions hold. **(i)** Its invariant is written down before
    the edit — what must be true afterwards that was true before. **(ii)** The invariant is
    computable in the sense of §B.2.20, so it can be checked rather than asserted. **(iii)** The
    edit is a *permutation or an insertion*, never a rewrite: existing text is moved, not retyped,
    so no character can change unnoticed. **(iv)** It is reversible — a copy is taken first and
    restored if the check fails. **(v)** It is checked afterwards on the source **and** the
    artefact, because §B.2.17.9's FIDELITY exists for the gap between them.

 **And a sixth that governs which repair to attempt: prefer the smallest edit that removes the
 defect.** A defect visible in a hundred places is not therefore a hundred-place repair. Applying
 that here changed what the repair was.

 B.2.21.1 The register, examined before repairing it
 The recorded defect was direction: entries 165 to 204 ascending, 205 onward descending. Measuring
 the register against its own headings found something larger and cheaper to fix. Each subsection of
 §21.7 states a count in its title — *Eight more*, *Twelve more*, *Fifteen more*, *Forty more* — and
 **§21.7.6 was titled "Three from the tower session" and contained eighty-six entries, 199 to 284**,
 every entry written since that session having been prepended into it. It is now four — the tower's
 three and register 202, which repairs their numbering — and §21.7.7 the eighty-seven written
 afterwards.

 **That is the defect worth repairing**, and it is one heading rather than a hundred and twenty
 entries. The direction is a presentation choice made twice; the heading is a false statement of
 count, which audit 15 ENUMERATION exists to catch and which it missed because it was pointed at
 tables and lists rather than at section titles. Registers 286 and 287.

 B.3 What the protocols are for
 Each prevents a specific failure, and each failure occurred:

  protocol                               failure it prevents                          instance
  B.2.1 channel construction             claiming cells across a label change         Si I, P II
  B.2.2 admissibility                    bracketing unresolved levels                 —
  B.2.3 cost resolvability               reading rounding as physics                  Al I nf
  B.2.4 dilution                         excluding a viable species                   Ar II, Bi I
  B.2.5 census first                     searching without targets                    27 sequences
                                                                                      enumerated
  B.2.6 declines recorded                an uncheckable collection                    Ne II, Cu II
  B.2.7 exhaustive testing               a claim resting on a sample                  A.4 on all cells
  B.2.8 two routes                       an undetectable derivation error             w = 3ν·e
  B.2.9 refuse, don't coerce             a missing value read as a real one           the cap discard
  B.2.10 retrieval                       abandoning a cell when a source is blocked   ρ = 6 vs ρ = 1
  B.2.11 provenance                      an untraceable number                        153 channels
  B.2.12 withdrawal                      an unfalsifiable record                      48 entries
  B.2.13 commit before you look          a choice that depended on its answer         the anchoring failure
  B.2.14 compute then write              the dominant failure                         most of Chapter 20
  B.2.15 apply P8 to every failure       a failure discarded rather than banked       ten bounds on §23.3

 **The protocols are not advice. They are the failure modes of this work, inverted.**

{"returncode":0,"stdout":"# PART 0 — THE SHAPE OF THE ARGUMENT

## Preface — the shape of the argument
 This book makes one claim, demonstrates it on one object, and reports every place the demonstration
 failed.

 **The claim.** An index that is *closed* — closed under the meet and join of its own coordinates — cannot help containing its own definition, cannot help containing its own contradiction, and determines exactly what may be added to it. These are not three properties that a well-made index happens to have. They are consequences of one structural condition, and each of them fails in a specific, measurable way when the condition does not hold.

 **The object.** Λ, an ordering of atomic electron configurations on eight coordinates. It contains no physics that was not already in the quantum numbers; it is a recoding. That is deliberate. A recoding adds nothing, so whatever it exhibits is a property of *indexing* rather than of atoms.

 **The demonstration.** A method that brackets Rydberg energy levels using only measured neighbours, tested on 1,442 interior cells across 35 atomic systems, spanning ℓ = 0 to 6 and *Z* = 1 to 83. The bracket holds in every one. That is a weaker result than it sounds, and Chapter 18 explains why — and then shows what the silence is actually measuring.

 The register. two hundred and ninety-seven claims made in the course of this work were wrong and were
 withdrawn. They are listed in Chapter 21, with what replaced them. Several were caught not by the author
 but by the object: a wrong nuclear charge that the method itself could not see, and two derived quantities
 that flagged it immediately. That episode is the book's best evidence, and it is an account of an
 error.

 Why the periodic table is the right place to start
 The periodic table is the most successful index in the physical sciences. It is also not closed, and the cost
 of that is exactly thirty-six cells.

 Chapter 1 computes it. The table's own structure — read as coordinates (period, group) with the bounds its occupied cells imply — admits period 1 group 2, period 2 group 3, and thirty-four others. They do not exist. **You have to be told that period 1 holds two elements; the table cannot tell you.**

 Λ is the same 118 elements. Its external definition cost is zero.

 That difference is the whole book. Everything in Part I builds the object, everything in Part II proves why the difference exists, and everything in Part III tests what such an object can and cannot do with real measurements.

 How to read this
 If you want the general result, Part II is self-contained. Chapter 9 defines closure; Chapters 10 to 12
 prove the three consequences; Chapter 13 states what none of it can deliver.

 **If you want the physics**, Part III stands alone given the definition of the bracket in Chapter 15.

 If you want to check the work, Chapter 21 and Appendix C are where the withdrawals and the
 provenance live. Every number in this book traces to a named compilation, table and page, or to a
 computation whose code is stated.

 **And if you are looking for a prediction**, there is none, and Chapter 18 explains why: what looks like one is a deduction from measured neighbours, offered as falsifiable rather than as a result. **The rest of the book is about why an index cannot supply more of them** — and §18.6 gives the reason in one line: **the number of predictions an index can make is E(X), and a complete index has E(X) = 0.**

 **That is not a limitation discovered late. It is what completeness means.** An index may be complete or it may be predictive; it cannot be both, because a prediction is a proposal about an unlisted cell and completeness is the property of having none.

# PART I — THE LATTICE
---CH2---
## 2. The construction of Λ
 Λ is a set of eight-tuples. Each is a transition cell: a source configuration, a target configuration, and the
 electron count moved between them.

      (n, ℓ, k, q, e, f, g, 2S)

| | |
|---|---|
| *n* | source shell |
| ℓ | source subshell |
| *k* | source occupancy |
| *q* | electrons removed |
| *e* | target shell |
| *f* | target subshell |
| *g* | target occupancy |
| 2*S* | multiplicity |

 Five further coordinates — 2S′, v, 2J_c, K and 2J — extend Λ₈ to Λ₁₃ when target spin, seniority and
 angular-momentum coupling are carried explicitly; §7.11 builds the tower and fixes the order, which is
 J_c, then K, then J. Everything in this book that does not concern coupling is stated for Λ₈.

 One row of the table below is not like the others. Three origins — Pauli, the hydrogenic solution,
 counting — yield exact constraints. The fourth, vector coupling, yields an envelope: 2S ≤ k contains
 every physical multiplicity and admits values no k electrons can carry, at 48.5% density at the caps of
 §2.4. §7.11.3 states the dichotomy and §7.11.2 proves it is forced.

### 2.1 The constraints, and where each comes from
 Λ is not all of the eight-fold product. It is the subset satisfying:

  constraint                      origin
  ℓ≤n−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
  k ≤ 2(2ℓ + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
  q≤k                             counting — cannot remove more than are present
  f≤e−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
  g ≤ 2(2f + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
  g≤q                             counting — cannot place more than were removed
  2S ≤ k                          vector coupling

 **Seven constraints, four origins, and nothing else.** No constraint in Λ comes from anywhere but Pauli, the hydrogenic radial solution, counting, or angular-momentum coupling. That exhaustiveness matters in Part II, where it is the reason the object's properties can be attributed to *indexing* rather than to physics smuggled in through a bound.

### 2.2 Every constraint is of one form
 Each constraint reads xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) — one coordinate bounded by a monotone function of one other. None is
 a sum. None is a difference. That is not an accident of presentation; Chapter 12 shows that a sum could
 not appear here, because a set cut out by a sum bound is not closed.

 **Consequence, developed in Chapter 3:** the graph whose nodes are coordinates and whose edges are constraints is a **tree**.

 Figure 2.1. Every constraint binds one coordinate to one other. Eight nodes, seven edges, connected — a tree, and
 therefore treewidth 1. Three results in this book follow from that fact alone.

### 2.3 Λ is closed
 For any two cells x, y ∈ Λ, both x ∨ y and x ∧ y — the coordinatewise maximum and minimum — are again
 in Λ.

 *Proof.* Each constraint is *xᵢ* ≤ φ(*xⱼ*) with φ non-decreasing. Suppose (*x*∨*y*)ᵢ = *xᵢ*. Then

    (x∨y)ᵢ = xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) ≤ φ(max(xⱼ, yⱼ)) = φ((x∨y)ⱼ)

 by monotonicity. Meets are symmetric. ∎

 And E(Λ) = 0, verified by direct computation at four cap settings — 216, 976, 1,636 and 2,394 cells —
 exact in one step and stable under a second application of ℛ.

### 2.4 A note on caps
 Λ is infinite; every count in this book is stated at explicit caps on n, e, ℓ and k. The counts change with
 the caps. The shape does not — a claim made precise in Chapter 3, where the generator patterns are
 shown identical across a twenty-eight-fold range in cell count.

 Where a number is cap-dependent it is marked. Where a structural claim is made, it has been checked at no fewer than four settings.

 Five further coordinates — 2S′, v, 2J_c, K and 2J — extend Λ₈ to Λ₁₃ when target spin, seniority and
 angular-momentum coupling are carried explicitly; §7.11 builds the tower and fixes the order, which is
 J_c, then K, then J. Everything in this book that does not concern coupling is stated for Λ₈.

 One row of the table below is not like the others. Three origins — Pauli, the hydrogenic solution,
 counting — yield exact constraints. The fourth, vector coupling, yields an envelope: 2S ≤ k contains
 every physical multiplicity and admits values no k electrons can carry, at 48.5% density at the caps of
 §2.4. §7.11.3 states the dichotomy and §7.11.2 proves it is forced.

### 2.1 The constraints, and where each comes from
 Λ is not all of the eight-fold product. It is the subset satisfying:

  constraint                      origin
  ℓ≤n−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
  k ≤ 2(2ℓ + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
  q≤k                             counting — cannot remove more than are present
  f≤e−1                           hydrogenic radial solution
  g ≤ 2(2f + 1)                   Pauli exclusion
  g≤q                             counting — cannot place more than were removed
  2S ≤ k                          vector coupling

 **Seven constraints, four origins, and nothing else.** No constraint in Λ comes from anywhere but Pauli, the hydrogenic radial solution, counting, or angular-momentum coupling. That exhaustiveness matters in Part II, where it is the reason the object's properties can be attributed to *indexing* rather than to physics smuggled in through a bound.

### 2.2 Every constraint is of one form
 Each constraint reads xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) — one coordinate bounded by a monotone function of one other. None is
 a sum. None is a difference. That is not an accident of presentation; Chapter 12 shows that a sum could
 not appear here, because a set cut out by a sum bound is not closed.

 **Consequence, developed in Chapter 3:** the graph whose nodes are coordinates and whose edges are constraints is a **tree**.

 Figure 2.1. Every constraint binds one coordinate to one other. Eight nodes, seven edges, connected — a tree, and
 therefore treewidth 1. Three results in this book follow from that fact alone.

### 2.3 Λ is closed
 For any two cells x, y ∈ Λ, both x ∨ y and x ∧ y — the coordinatewise maximum and minimum — are again
 in Λ.

 *Proof.* Each constraint is *xᵢ* ≤ φ(*xⱼ*) with φ non-decreasing. Suppose (*x*∨*y*)ᵢ = *xᵢ*. Then

    (x∨y)ᵢ = xᵢ ≤ φ(xⱼ) ≤ φ(max(xⱼ, yⱼ)) = φ((x∨y)ⱼ)

 by monotonicity. Meets are symmetric. ∎

 And E(Λ) = 0, verified by direct computation at four cap settings — 216, 976, 1,636 and 2,394 cells —
 exact in one step and stable under a second application of ℛ.

### 2.4 A note on caps
 Λ is infinite; every count in this book is stated at explicit caps on n, e, ℓ and k. The counts change with
 the caps. The shape does not — a claim made precise in Chapter 3, where the generator patterns are
 shown identical across a twenty-eight-fold range in cell count.

 Where a number is cap-dependent it is marked. Where a structural claim is made, it has been checked at no fewer than four settings.

content.text:
This is often addressed by means of Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA).

**Results:**

We put forward a framework in which GED analysis is understood as an Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA) process where we provide support for continuous human interaction with data aiming at improving the step of hypothesis abduction and assessment. We focus on the adaptation to human cognition of data interpretation and visualization of the output of EDA.

First, we give a proper theoretical background to bi-clustering using Lattice Theory and provide a set of analysis tools revolving around $\mathcal {K}$-Formal Concept Analysis ($\mathcal {K}$-FCA), a lattice-theoretic unsupervised learning technique for real-valued matrices.

By using different kinds of cost structures to quantify expression we obtain different sequences of hierarchical bi-clusterings for gene under- and over-expression using thresholds. 

Consequently, we provide a method with interleaved analysis steps and visualization devices so that the sequences of lattices for a particular experiment summarize the researcher’s vision of the data. This also allows us to define measures of persistence and robustness of biclusters to assess them.

Second, the resulting biclusters are used to index external omics databases—for instance, Gene Ontology (GO)—thus offering a new way of accessing publicly available resources. This provides different flavors of gene set enrichment against which to assess the biclusters, by obtaining their *p*-values according to the terminology of those resources.

We illustrate the exploration procedure on a real data example confirming results previously published.

**Conclusions:**

The GED analysis problem gets transformed into the exploration of a sequence of lattices enabling the visualization of the hierarchical structure of the biclusters with a certain degree of granularity.

# The Hypercube Structure of the Genetic Code Explains Conservative and Non-Conservative Aminoacid Substitutions in vivo and in vitro

Miguel A. Jiménez-Montaño\* Departamento de Física y Matemáticas, Universidad de las Américas, Puebla, Sta. Catarina Mártir, 72820 Cholula, Puebla, México

Carlos R. de la Mora-Basáñez<sup>+</sup>

Xalapa, Ver. 91000, México

#### Thorsten Pöschel\*\*

Arbeitsgruppe Nichtlineare Dynamik, Universität Potsdam, Am Neuen Palais, D-14415 Potsdam, Germany, and The James Franck Institute, University of Chicago, 5640 South Ellis Avenue, Chicago, Illinois 60637 (October 28, 2018)

A representation of the genetic code as a six-dimensional Boolean hypercube is described. This structure is the result of the hierarchical order of the interaction energies of the bases in codon–anticodon recognition. In this paper it is applied to study molecular evolution in vivo and in vitro. 

In the first case we compared aligned positions in homologous protein sequences and found two different behaviors: a) There are sites in which the different amino acids may be explained by one or two "attractor nodes" (coding for the dominating amino acid(s)) and their one–bit neighbors in the codon hypercube, and b) There are sites in which the amino acids correspond to codons located in closed paths in the hypercube. In the second case we studied the "Sexual PCR" experiment described by Stemmer [1] and found that the success of this combination of usual PCR and recombination is in part due to the Gray code structure of the genetic code.

content.title: A New DNA Sequences Vector Space on a Genetic Code Galois Field
content.text:
#### 1. Introduction

Recently was reported the Boolean lattices of the genetic code (Sánchez et al. 2004a and 2004b). Two dual genetic code Boolean lattices –primal and dual- were obtained as the direct third power of the two dual Boolean lattices B(X) of the four DNA bases: $C(X)=B(X)\times B(X)\times B(X)$ . The most elemental properties of the DNA bases and amino acids were used to establish the Boolean lattices B(X) which are isomorphic to $((Z_2)^2, \vee, \wedge)$ and $((Z_2)^2, \wedge, \vee)$ ( $Z_2=\{0,1\}$ ). Consequently, the lattices C(X) are isomorphic to the dual Boolean lattices $((Z_2)^6, \vee, \wedge)$ and $((Z_2)^6, \wedge, \vee)$ .

Here, we is used the isomorphism $\varphi: B(X) \rightarrow (Z_2)^2$ and the biological importance of base positions in the codons to state a partial order in the codon set and represent the codons as a binary sextuplet. The importance of the base position is suggested by the error frequency found in the codons.

content.title: Reference genome - Wikipedia
content.text:
The latest human reference genome assembly, released by the Genome Reference Consortium, was GRCh38 in 2017. Several patches were added to update it, the latest patch being GRCh38.p14, published in March 2022. This build only has 349 gaps across the entire assembly, which implies a great improvement in comparison with the first version, which had roughly 150,000 gaps. The gaps are mostly in areas such as telomeres, centromeres, and long repetitive sequences, with the biggest gap along the long arm of the Y chromosome, a region of ~30 Mb in length (~52% of the Y chromosome's length). The number

As they are assembled from the sequencing of DNA from a number of individual donors, reference genomes do not accurately represent the set of genes of any single individual organism. Instead a reference provides a haploid mosaic of different DNA sequences from each donor. For example, the most recent human reference genome (assembly GRCh38/hg38) is derived from >60 genomic clone libraries.

There have now been 20 releases of the human reference genome by the year of 2013. Considerable improvements have been made with each release of the reference. One of the major novel technical advances GRCh38 used is the application of hydatidiform moles, which is a type of abnormal pregnancy that occurs when a sperm fertilizes an egg without nuclear DNA. The sperm then replicates its own DNA, resulting in two identical copies of each chromosome, which therefore does do not have any allelic variation and is ideal for generating unambiguous reads in highly homologous regions. The latest release GRCh38 is of course still not a perfect representation of the human reference genome. One of the major categories of unresolved regions in GRCh38 are the centromeres, which are millions of bases long and highly repetitive.

meta-dc.description: Basic parameters commonly used to describe genomes including length, weight and relative guanine-cytosine (GC) content are widely cited in absence of a primary source. By using updated data and original software we determined these values to the best of our knowledge as standard reference for the whole human nuclear genome, for each chromosome and for mitochondrial DNA. We also devised a method to calculate the relative GC content in the whole messenger RNA sequence set and in transcriptomes by multiplying the GC content of each gene by its mean expression level. The male nuclear diploid genome extends for 6.27 Gigabase pairs (Gbp), is 205.00&nbsp;cm (cm) long and weighs 6.41 picograms (pg). Female values are 6.37 Gbp, 208.23&nbsp;cm, 6.51&nbsp;pg. The individual variability and the implication for the DNA informational density in terms of bits/volume were discussed. The genomic GC content is 40.9%. Following analysis in different transcriptomes and species, we showed that the greatest deviation was observed in the pathological condition analysed (trisomy 21 leukaemic cells) and in Caenorhabditis elegans. Our results may represent a solid basis for further investigation on human structural and functional genomics while also providing a framework for other genome comparative analysis.

## Abstract

### Objective

Basic parameters commonly used to describe genomes including length, weight and relative guanine-cytosine (GC) content are widely cited in absence of a primary source. By using updated data and original software we determined these values to the best of our knowledge as standard reference for the whole human nuclear genome, for each chromosome and for mitochondrial DNA. We also devised a method to calculate the relative GC content in the whole messenger RNA sequence set and in transcriptomes by multiplying the GC content of each gene by its mean expression level.

### Results

The male nuclear diploid genome extends for 6.27 Gigabase pairs (Gbp), is 205.00 cm (cm) long and weighs 6.41 picograms (pg). Female values are 6.37 Gbp, 208.23 cm, 6.51 pg. The individual variability and the implication for the DNA informational density in terms of bits/volume were discussed. The genomic GC content is 40.9%. Following analysis in different transcriptomes and species, we showed that the greatest deviation was observed in the pathological condition analysed (trisomy 21 leukaemic cells) and in *Caenorhabditis elegans*. Our results may represent a solid basis for further investigation on human structural and functional genomics while also providing a framework for other genome comparative analysis.

The availability of a high-quality reference sequence for the human genome currently offers the possibility to provide an accurate evaluation of these parameters. In this work we propose revised estimations for the length, weight and GC content of the reference human genome and of individual chromosomes, including mtDNA, in a standard human diploid cell and in a reference human being. Moreover, in this paper we discuss the meaning of the obtained results and we formulated a method to calculate the relative GC content in the whole messenger RNA set of sequences and in transcriptomes, comparing different tissues and organisms.

## Main text

### Methods

#### Human genome length and weight calculations

Lengths in centimeters (cm) and weight in picograms (pg) of all 24 human chromosome and mtDNA sequences were calculated as detailed in Additional file [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM1): Additional Methods.

#### GC content analysis

The genomic GC content was calculated among the certain bases for the 24 chromosomes and for mtDNA as detailed in Additional file [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM1): Additional Methods.

The “Transcriptomic GC Analysis” (TGCA) software was developed here to study the possible variation of GC content in the expression of whole transcriptomes.

Human quantitative transcriptome maps were previously obtained from publicly available microarray datasets analysed through TRAM (Transcriptome Mapper) software [[30](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR30 "Lenzi L, Facchin F, Piva F, Giulietti M, Pelleri MC, Frabetti F, Vitale L, Casadei R, Canaider S, Bortoluzzi S, et al. TRAM (Transcriptome Mapper): database-driven creation and analysis of transcriptome maps from multiple sources. BMC Genomics. 2011;12:121.")] as described [[31](#ref-CR31 "Caracausi M, Vitale L, Pelleri MC, Piovesan A, Bruno S, Strippoli P. A quantitative transcriptome reference map of the normal human brain. Neurogenetics. 2014;15:267–87."),[32](#ref-CR32 "Pelleri MC, Piovesan A, Caracausi M, Berardi AC, Vitale L, Strippoli P. Integrated differential transcriptome maps of acute megakaryoblastic leukemia (AMKL) in children with or without Down Syndrome (DS). BMC Med Genomics. 2014;7:63."),[33](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR33 "Caracausi M, Rigon V, Piovesan A, Strippoli P, Vitale L, Pelleri MC. A quantitative transcriptome reference map of the normal human hippocampus. Hippocampus. 2016;26:13–26.")]. Since quantitative gene expression values may anticipate mutational effects that will most likely affect a given human tissue [[34](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR34 "Caracausi M, Piovesan A, Vitale L, Pelleri MC. Integrated transcriptome map highlights structural and functional aspects of the normal human Heart. J Cell Physiol. 2017;232:759–70.")], we compared a pathologic cell type with its normal counterpart and a whole organ with one of its subregions (Additional file [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM1): Additional Methods). For each analysis, only genes for which an expression value is available in both biological conditions were used. For each gene, the longest human mRNA sequence was obtained from the latest version of human 5′_ORF_Extender software [[35](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR35 "Casadei R, Piovesan A, Vitale L, Facchin F, Pelleri MC, Canaider S, Bianconi E, Frabetti F, Strippoli P. Genome-scale analysis of human mRNA 5′ coding sequences based on expressed sequence tag (EST) database. Genomics. 2012;100:125–30.")] (Additional file [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM1): Additional Methods).

Since TRAM and 5′_ORF_Extender were implemented for other organisms [[36](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR36 "Piovesan A, Vitale L, Pelleri MC, Strippoli P. Universal tight correlation of codon bias and pool of RNA codons (codonome): The genome is optimized to allow any distribution of gene expression values in the transcriptome from bacteria to humans. Genomics. 2013;101:282–9."), [37](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR37 "Piovesan A, Caracausi M, Pelleri MC, Vitale L, Martini S, Bassani C, Gurioli A, Casadei R, Solda G, Strippoli P. Improving mRNA 5′ coding sequence determination in the mouse genome. Mamm Genome. 2014;25:149–59.")], TGCA software itself was implemented with the purpose to be easily used with any sequence and expression dataset of any organism. Thus, we performed GC calculations on other representative species genomes: *Danio rerio*, *Caenorhabditis elegans*, *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* and *Escherichia coli* (Additional file [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM1): Additional Methods).

### Results

#### Human nuclear genome length and weight

Individual chromosome lengths in bp and cm are given in Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab2). Certain base counts and uncertain base composition estimations given in Additional file [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM2): Table S1 were used to calculate each chromosome weight, obtaining the results shown in Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab2). The length and weight sums of the 24 chromosomes (22 autosomes and X and Y chromosomes) were used in order to proportionately estimate the length and weight of the unplaced bases, improving whole genome calculation accuracy (Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab2)). Data for the previous assembly (GRCh37.p13) are also given in Additional file [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM3): Table S2 and Additional file [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM4): Table S3. The chromosomes varying to a greater extent between the two assembly versions are chromosomes 9 and Y (GRCh38 has 2.8 Mb and 2.1 Mb less than GRCh37, respectively) and chromosomes 17 and 18 (GRCh38 has 2.1 Mb and 2.3 Mb more than GRCh37, respectively).

Considering a mean length in a diploid cell of 206.62 cm and the latest estimation of a mean of 3 × 1012 nucleated cells for a reference human being [[38](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR38 "Bianconi E, Piovesan A, Facchin F, Beraudi A, Casadei R, Frabetti F, Vitale L, Pelleri MC, Tassani S, Piva F, et al. An estimation of the number of cells in the human body. Ann Hum Biol. 2013;40:463–71."), [39](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR39 "Sender R, Fuchs S, Milo R. Revised estimates for the number of human and bacteria cells in the body. PLoS Biol. 2016;14:e1002533.")], the total extension in length of all nuclear DNA molecules present in a single human individual is of about 6.20 billion km (6.20 × 1012 m) and is sufficient to cover the Earth-Sun distance (<https://cneos.jpl.nasa.gov/glossary/au.html>) more than 41 times. Considering a mean weight in a diploid cell of 6.46 pg, the genome weight summed across nucleated human cells would be about 19.39 g, almost the weight of 100 carats (<https://sizes.com/units/carat.htm>).

#### The mitochondrial genome

Applying all the calculations previously performed for the nuclear genome, the human mtDNA length, weight and GC content were estimated (Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab2)).

On average, a human cell could contain from a minimum of 2,845,394 ± 204,296 bp, 0.09 ± 0.0067 cm and 0.0029 ± 0.00021 pg to a maximum of 110,742,060 ± 4,568,736.06 bp, 3.62 ± 0.15 cm and 0.11 ± 0.0047 pg of mtDNA in total, depending on the uncertainty of the number DNA molecules per cell [[40](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR40 "D’Erchia AM, Atlante A, Gadaleta G, Pavesi G, Chiara M, De Virgilio C, Manzari C, Mastropasqua F, Prazzoli GM, Picardi E, et al. Tissue-specific mtDNA abundance from exome data and its correlation with mitochondrial transcription, mass and respiratory activity. Mitochondrion. 2015;20:13–21.")] (Additional file [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM1): Additional Methods). Therefore, the mtDNA, despite its size being greatly reduced in comparison to those of nuclear DNA (1/195,663 compared to haploid nuclear genome), constitutes a significant share of total DNA of a human cell: about 0.90–1.21% (diploid cell), being able to represent at least 52.03% of the DNA in the case of a mature oocyte.

#### GC content analysis

The human GC contents calculated among the certain bases (A, T, W, G, C, and S) counted in the 24 human chromosomes excluding the 150,630,700 uncertain bases are shown in Table [2](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab2) (Additional file [4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM4): Table S3 for GRCh37.p13). Among the other investigated species, the calculated chromosome numbers, total genome bp lengths and genomic GC contents (Table [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab3)) are in accordance with previous reports (Additional file [5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM5): Table S4).

Human Down Syndrome (DS) Acute Megakaryoblastic Leukemia (AMKL) blasts and euploid megakaryoblasts (MK) transcriptome maps have an expression value in both conditions together with mRNA sequences available for 16,547 genes. This value for whole human hippocampus and whole brain transcriptome maps is of 17,579 genes. Among the other investigated species, this value is of 6642 genes for *D. rerio* brain, 19,281 for *C. elegans*, 4673 for *S. cerevisiae* and 2426 for *E. coli*. The mRNA GC contents calculated in these subsets using TGCA software are given in Table [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab3). For each biological condition, each mRNA GC absolute count was then multiplied by the corresponding expression value. The sum of these values related to each transcriptome map gives the transcriptomic GC content (Table [3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab3)). mRNA and transcriptomic GC contents for each chromosome in DS-AMKL and MK conditions are given in Additional file [6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM6): Table S5. DS-AMKL condition has 7 chromosomes (9, 11, 20, 17, 16, 22, 19) with a transcriptomic GC content higher than 48.80 which is the total mRNA GC % (the maximum is 56.26% of chr19), while MK condition has 9 chromosomes (7, 15, 9, 11, 20, 17, 22, 16, 19) with a transcriptomic GC content higher than that value (the maximum is 59.02% of chr19, which is a very high value).

### Discussion

In this work we have determined, to the best of our knowledge, basic parameters describing the normal human reference genome: the length, expressed in terms of both bp and unit of length (cm, m), weight (in unit of mass, pg) and relative GC content expressed in percentages, for the whole human nuclear genome, for each chromosome and for mtDNA.

We have based our calculations on the GRCh38 assembly, which is longer and more contiguous than previous reference assembly versions and provides a sequence-based representation for genomic features such as centromeres and telomeres for the first time [[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR5 "Schneider VA, Graves-Lindsay T, Howe K, Bouk N, Chen HC, Kitts PA, Murphy TD, Pruitt KD, Thibaud-Nissen F, Albracht D, et al. Evaluation of GRCh38 and de novo haploid genome assemblies demonstrates the enduring quality of the reference assembly. Genome Res. 2017;27:849–64.")], which, although variable among cell types and ages, would affect our estimates to a small extent. However, the human genetic diversity ranges from the single-nucleotide variation to large chromosomal events [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR41 "Alkan C, Coe BP, Eichler EE. Genome structural variation discovery and genotyping. Nat Rev Genet. 2011;12:363–76."), [42](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR42 "Sudmant PH, Rausch T, Gardner EJ, Handsaker RE, Abyzov A, Huddleston J, Zhang Y, Ye K, Jun G, Hsi-Yang Fritz M, et al. An integrated map of structural variation in 2504 human genomes. Nature. 2015;526:75–81.")]. Following the sequencing of 1000 human genomes [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR43 "Auton A, Brooks LD, Durbin RM, Garrison EP, Kang HM, Korbel JO, Marchini JL, McCarthy S, McVean GA, Abecasis GR. A global reference for human genetic variation. Nature. 2015;526:68–74.")], a recent analysis estimated ~ 20 million bases of sequence variation in a typical diploid genome [[43](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR43 "Auton A, Brooks LD, Durbin RM, Garrison EP, Kang HM, Korbel JO, Marchini JL, McCarthy S, McVean GA, Abecasis GR. A global reference for human genetic variation. Nature. 2015;526:68–74.")]. Applying this order of magnitude of variation to our estimates, a proportional variability among individuals of ± 0.65 cm and 0.02 pg for the length and weight of a human mean diploid genome can be assumed.

Our results are not far from previous rough estimates (Table [1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#Tab1)), however the more accurate determination of the human genome length and weight might offer interesting possibilities. A recent analysis of 70 genomes from prokaryotes to primates showed that five informational laws about genome structure complexity may have been found [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR44 "Bonnici V, Manca V. Informational laws of genome structures. Sci Rep. 2016;6:28840.")], suggested by indexes based on the value k = lg2(n), where k is the length of a string occurring in the genome and n is the genome length [[44](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR44 "Bonnici V, Manca V. Informational laws of genome structures. Sci Rep. 2016;6:28840.")]. Applying our analysis to other genomes would be useful to update these indexes. Another interesting possibility offered by the knowledge of human nuclear genome length is the derivation of the total human DNA volume, in order to estimate the efficiency of DNA in data storage, resulted to be in the order of 104 fold superior in comparison to the most currently advanced hard disks (Additional file [7](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#MOESM7): Discussion). The genome weight is a parameter useful for the correlation with the DNA extraction yields through different methods [[45](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR45 "Preis M, Schneiderman J, Koren B, Ben-Yosef Y, Levin-Ashkenazi D, Shapiro S, Cohen T, Blich M, Israeli-Amit M, Sarnatzki Y, et al. Co-expression of fibulin-5 and VEGF165 increases long-term patency of synthetic vascular grafts seeded with autologous endothelial cells. Gene Ther. 2016;23:237–46.")].

Regarding GC content analysis at genomic level, our results are in agreement with a recent study [[6](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR6 "Guo Y, Dai Y, Yu H, Zhao S, Samuels DC, Shyr Y. Improvements and impacts of GRCh38 human reference on high throughput sequencing data analysis. Genomics. 2017;109:83–90.")]. Through the implementation of TGCA software we have also determined the GC content at mRNA and transcriptomic levels for the first time, a novel concept we propose here, which is the GC percentage calculated in the mRNA amount actually expressed in a tissue. The human genomic GC content results to be much lower than mRNA GC content. mRNA GC content is in turn similar to the transcriptomic GC content. This has been confirmed also in *D. rerio* and *C. elegans* and to a lesser extent in *S. cerevisiae* and in *E. coli*. Overall, it seems that the GC composition of highly and poorly expressed genes in specific tissues affects the mRNA GC content to a small extent and a global compensation between them may exist.

Comparing different biological conditions, the greatest deviation from the mRNA GC content was found in a condition of aneuploidy and leukaemia (DS-AMKL). Interestingly, DS-AMKL transcriptomic GC content skews in a greater extent from the transcriptomic GC content of the healthy euploid counterpart of MK cells. Recent works conducted on DS subjects showed typical alterations of the metabolome and whole transcriptome [[46](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR46 "Caracausi M, Ghini V, Locatelli C, Mericio M, Piovesan A, Antonaros F, Pelleri MC, Vitale L, Vacca RA, Bedetti F, et al. Plasma and urinary metabolomic profiles of Down Syndrome correlate with alteration of mitochondrial metabolism. Sci Rep. 2018;8:2977."), [47](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR47 "Pelleri MC, Cattani C, Vitale L, Antonaros F, Strippoli P, Locatelli C, Cocchi G, Piovesan A, Caracausi M. Integrated quantitative transcriptome maps of human trisomy 21 tissues and cells. Front Genet. 2018;9:125.")]. Chromosome 21 GC content is one of the closest to the mean genomic GC content, thus the presence of a third copy of chromosome 21 would not cause a great change in GC composition at genomic level. Since the duplication of at least a restricted region of human chromosome 21 is associated to DS [[48](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR48 "Pelleri MC, Cicchini E, Locatelli C, Vitale L, Caracausi M, Piovesan A, Rocca A, Poletti G, Seri M, Strippoli P, et al. Systematic reanalysis of partial trisomy 21 cases with or without Down Syndrome suggests a small region on 21q22.13 as critical to the phenotype. Hum Mol Genet. 2016;25:2525–38.")], further studies are necessary to determine whether the duplication of this chromosome 21 region and/or the leukaemia condition is responsible for this deviation pattern. For example, a recent work showed a high expression of high-GC-content mRNAs in psoriasis lesion transcriptome, while resolving lesions had a low expression of these mRNAs [[49](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR49 "Swindell WR, Xing X, Voorhees JJ, Elder JT, Johnston A, Gudjonsson JE. Integrative RNA-seq and microarray data analysis reveals GC content and gene length biases in the psoriasis transcriptome. Physiol Genomics. 2014;46:533–46.")]. More in-depth analysis will be needed to validate the use of these indexes as indicators in the comparison of disease versus normal conditions.

Genomic, mRNA and transcriptomic GC content determination can be useful in DNA and RNA sequencing analyses where GC content bias for the Illumina sequencing technology has been documented as likely introduced at the library preparation step, resulting in confounding DNA copy number studies and expression fold-change estimates [[50](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR50 "Risso D, Schwartz K, Sherlock G, Dudoit S. GC-content normalization for RNA-Seq data. BMC Bioinformatics. 2011;12:480.")].

In conclusion, we provide an update on fundamental human genome parameters and a first characterisation of the mRNA and transcriptome GC contents. Our results may represent a solid basis for further investigations on human structural and functional genomics [[29](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR29 "Piovesan A, Caracausi M, Ricci M, Strippoli P, Vitale L, Pelleri MC. Identification of minimal eukaryotic introns through GeneBase, a user-friendly tool for parsing the NCBI Gene databank. DNA Res. 2015;22:495–503."), [51](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR51 "Piovesan A, Caracausi M, Antonaros F, Pelleri MC, Vitale L. GeneBase 1.1: a tool to summarize data from NCBI Gene datasets and its application to an update of human gene statistics. Database Oxford. 2016;2016:baw153.")] while also providing a framework for the comparative analysis of other genomes.

## Limitations

Determination of the length, weight and relative GC content of genome is subjected to the accuracy of the genome assembly and to the variability existing among individuals [[41](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR41 "Alkan C, Coe BP, Eichler EE. Genome structural variation discovery and genotyping. Nat Rev Genet. 2011;12:363–76.")]. Regarding mtDNA, although its sequence has been exactly determined, the mtDNA molecule copy number per cell is of difficult estimation [[52](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR52 "Bogenhagen DF. Mitochondrial DNA nucleoid structure. Biochim Biophys Acta. 2012;1819:914–20.")]. Regarding GC content at mRNA and transcriptomic levels, the analysis is limited to genes for which an expression value together with the corresponding longest mRNA nucleotide sequence is publicly available. Finally, mRNA 5´ region is known to have a composition bias [[53](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR53 "Pesole G, Liuni S, Grillo G, Saccone C. Structural and compositional features of untranslated regions of eukaryotic mRNAs. Gene. 1997;205:95–102.")] and a better delimitation of this sequence may be necessary [[54](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s13104-019-4137-z#ref-CR54 "Vitale L, Caracausi M, Casadei R, Pelleri MC, Piovesan A. Difficulty in obtaining the complete mRNA coding sequence at 5′ region (5′ end mRNA artifact): causes, consequences in biology and medicine and possible solutions for obtaining the actual amino acid sequence of proteins (Review). Int J Mol Med. 2017;39:1063–71.")].

### Availability of data and materials

The datasets generated and analysed during the current study are publicly available online at <http://apollo11.isto.unibo.it/software/>. Some of them are also are available within the article and its additional information files.

The Python executable script used to count any type of nucleotide letter, the FileMaker stand-alone database with which the counts were analysed and the tutorial are publicly available at <http://apollo11.isto.unibo.it/software/>.

TGCA software was developed within the FileMaker Pro Advanced environment (FileMaker, Santa Clara, CA, version 12). Mac OS X and Windows stand-alone software (TGCA versions pre-loaded with transcriptome and sequence data and empty) are freely available to all for basic use at <http://apollo11.isto.unibo.it/software/>, including the FileMaker runtime and a tutorial.

Project name: TGCA_Software.

Project home page: <http://apollo11.isto.unibo.it/software/>.

Programming language: Python and FileMaker.

Operating systems: Mac OS X and Windows.

Minimum software requirements: Mac OS X 10.6, OS X Lion 10.7, OS X Mountain Lion 10.8; Windows XP Professional, Home Edition (Service Pack 3); Windows Vista Ultimate, Business, Home Premium (Service Pack 2); Windows 7 Ultimate, Professional, Home Premium; Windows 8 Standard and Pro edition.

Minimum system requirements: Mac OS X 10.6, Intel-based Mac CPU (Central Processing Unit), 1 GigaByte (GB) of RAM (Random Access Memory), 1024 × 768 or higher resolution video adapter and display. Windows XP Professional, Home Edition (Service Pack 3), 700 MegaHertz (MHz) CPU or faster, 256 MegaBytes (MB) of RAM, 1024 × 768 or higher resolution video adapter and display.

A connection to the Internet is required to display the software tutorial and to download data for set up, but not to run the tool.

Any restrictions to use by non-academics: freely available to all for basic use.

E(X) = |R(X)| - |X|, R = closure under coordinatewise join and meet.
"""

# ---- PROVENANCE NOTE (B.2.11) --------------------------------------------
# GRCh38 chromInfo lengths below are RECALLED, not retrieved this session.
# The fetch of the Piovesan et al. 2019 Table 2 returned the article body
# without the table. This is a STATED GAP in the B.2.10 sense, not a silent
# default. Every STRUCTURAL result below is tested for dependence on the
# exact values (see test_stability).
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------

L = {  # GRCh38 primary assembly, bp
 1:248956422, 2:242193529, 3:198295559, 4:190214555, 5:181538259,
 6:170805979, 7:159345973, 8:145138636, 9:138394717, 10:133797422,
 11:135086622,12:133275309,13:114364328,14:107043718,15:101991189,
 16:90338345, 17:83257441, 18:80373285, 19:58617616, 20:64444167,
 21:46709983, 22:50818468, 23:156040895, 24:57227415}   # 23=X, 24=Y
NAME = {23:'X',24:'Y'}
def nm(c): return NAME.get(c,str(c))

order = sorted(L)                     # the conventional labelling 1..22,X,Y
lens  = [L[c] for c in order]
N_occ = sum(lens)

# Cells: (c, p) with 1 <= p <= L(c).  Join = (max c, max p), meet = (min,min).
# By the running-maxima characterisation (B.2.15.2 / sec 23.3):
#   R(X) = {(c,p) : p <= M(c)},  M(c) = max_{c' <= c} L(c')
def closure_size(lengths):
    M, run = [], 0
    for x in lengths:
        run = max(run, x); M.append(run)
    return sum(M), M

R_size, M = closure_size(lens)
E_pos = R_size - N_occ

print("=== 1. THE (chromosome, position) INDEX ===")
print(f"|X|      = {N_occ:,}   (occupied cells = assembled bases)")
print(f"|R(X)|   = {R_size:,}")
print(f"E(X)     = {E_pos:,}")
print(f"E/|X|    = {E_pos/N_occ:.4f}")
print(f"running max is constant at chr1 length: {len(set(M))==1}")

    """brute-force join/meet closure test over all pairs of extreme cells"""
    n = len(lengths); bad = []
    for i in range(n):
        for j in range(n):
            # extreme cell of i joined with extreme cell of j
            c, p = max(i,j), max(lengths[i], lengths[j])
            if p > lengths[c]:
                bad.append((i,j,c,p,lengths[c]))
    return bad

print(f"\njoin-closure violations over {len(lens)**2} ordered pairs: {len(bad)}")
print("first three witnesses (0-indexed chrom slots):")
for w in bad[:3]:
    i,j,c,p,cap = w
    print(f"   chr{nm(order[i])} v chr{nm(order[j])} -> (chr{nm(order[c])}, {p:,}) but L=({cap:,})")

# --- the test must be shown capable of returning clean:
sorted_lens = sorted(lens)
print(f"violations after sorting by length: {len(is_closed(sorted_lens))}  <-- test can return 0")

# ---- 3. E after the relabelling ------------------------------------------

print(f"\n=== 2. AFTER SORTING CHROMOSOMES BY LENGTH ===")
print(f"|X| = {sum(sorted_lens):,}   |R(X)| = {R2:,}   E = {R2-sum(sorted_lens):,}")

inv = [(order[i],order[j]) for i in range(len(lens)) for j in range(i+1,len(lens))
       if lens[i] < lens[j]]
aut = [p for p in inv if p[0]<=22 and p[1]<=22]
print(f"\n=== 3. REORDERABILITY (sec 23.3) ===")
print(f"total inversions in the conventional order: {len(inv)}")
print(f"inversions among the 22 autosomes only:     {len(aut)}")
print(f"autosome inversions: {[(nm(a),nm(b)) for a,b in aut]}")

# ---- 5. stability of the structural claim under perturbed lengths --------
import random
def test_stability(trials=2000):
    random.seed(11); fails=0
    for _ in range(trials):
        pert = [int(x*random.uniform(0.90,1.10)) for x in lens]
        if len(is_closed(pert))==0: fails+=1
    return fails
print(f"\nstability: closed under +-10% length perturbation in "
      f"{test_stability()} of 2000 trials  (structural claim independent of exact bp)")

import random, math
random.seed(7)

# ---- 4. THE SEQUENCE AS AN INDEX -----------------------------------------
# The (chr,pos) index carries POSITIONS. It does not carry BASES.
# Adjoin the base axis: cells are (p, b), b in {A,C,G,T} -> {0,1,2,3}.
# The genome is the GRAPH OF A FUNCTION p -> b_p : exactly one base per site.

def R_twoaxis(cells, nmax, bmax):
    """closure under coordinatewise join+meet, computed to fixed point"""
    S = set(cells)
    while True:
        new = set()
        for x in S:
            for y in S:
                new.add((max(x[0],y[0]), max(x[1],y[1])))
                new.add((min(x[0],y[0]), min(x[1],y[1])))
        if new <= S: return S
        S |= new

def E_sequence(seq):
    cells = [(i, b) for i, b in enumerate(seq)]
    return len(R_twoaxis(cells, len(seq), 4)) - len(cells)

print("=== 4. E OF THE SEQUENCE CONTENT ===")
for N in (50, 200, 800):
    seq = [random.randrange(4) for _ in range(N)]
    E = E_sequence(seq)
    print(f"  N={N:4d}  E={E:5d}   E/N = {E/N:.4f}   (|S|-1 = 3)")

# monotone (sorted) sequence -- the only closed case
for N in (50, 200, 800):
    seq = sorted(random.randrange(4) for _ in range(N))
    print(f"  N={N:4d}  E={E_sequence(seq):5d}  <-- sorted sequence (AAA..CCC..GGG..TTT)")

# ---- the identity, extrapolated ------------------------------------------
N_gen = 3_088_269_832
E_gen = 3 * N_gen
bits  = N_gen * math.log2(3 + 1)
print(f"\n  human genome: E = 3N = {E_gen:,}")
print(f"  description length = N*log2(E/N + 1) = {bits:,.0f} bits = {bits/8/1e6:,.0f} MB")

# ---- 5. THE TWO BRANCHES, AND WHERE THEY CROSS (sec 16.9.2) ---------------
print("\n=== 5. THE k-MER CROSSING ===")
N = N_gen
print("   k   4^k (alphabet cap)      N-k+1 (length cap)     binding")
kstar = None
for k in range(12, 21):
    a, b = 4**k, N - k + 1
    binding = "alphabet" if a < b else "length"
    if a >= b and kstar is None: kstar = k
    print(f"  {k:3d}   {a:>22,}   {b:>19,}   {binding}")
print(f"\n  branches cross at k* = log_4(N) = {math.log(N,4):.3f}")
print(f"  first integer k where the alphabet cap ceases to bind: {kstar}")

# ---- 6. DOES THE RELABELLED INDEX CARRY ITS OWN BOUNDS? (S3, sec 10.2) ----
print("\n=== 6. S3 -- ARE THE BOUNDS RECOVERABLE FROM THE CELLS? ===")
Ltest = [10, 7, 13, 4]                      # unsorted toy 'chromosomes'
X = {(c,p) for c,l in enumerate(Ltest) for p in range(1, l+1)}
recovered = [max(p for (cc,p) in X if cc==c) for c in range(len(Ltest))]
print(f"  declared bounds : {Ltest}")
print(f"  recovered by max: {recovered}   S3 holds: {recovered==Ltest}")
RX = R_twoaxis(X, None, None)
rec_after = [max(p for (cc,p) in RX if cc==c) for c in range(len(Ltest))]
print(f"  after applying R: {rec_after}   <-- closure OVERWROTE the true bounds")
print(f"  E = {len(RX)-len(X)}")
EOF

Distinguished structural invariants from contingent artifacts through rigorous perturbation testing.

content.text:
## Verdict: not closed, and — this is the finding — it cannot be closed without destroying its content.

**The (chromosome, position) index, computed.** Cells are (c, p) with 1 ≤ p ≤ L(c). Join is (max c, max p).

| | |
|---|---|
| \|X\| | 3,088,269,832 |
| \|ℛ(X)\| | 5,974,954,128 |
| **E(X)** | **2,886,684,296** |
| E/\|X\| | 0.9347 |

512 of 576 ordered pairs violate join closure. The running maximum is constant — chr1 is both first and longest — so ℛ(X) is the *entire ambient box*. This is Chapter 1's thirty-six cells at 80 million times the scale: you have to be told that chr21 stops at 46.7 Mb; the coordinate system cannot tell you.

**The repair is a relabelling, and it is exact.** Sorting chromosomes by length makes L non-decreasing, φ monotone, and §2.3's proof goes through unchanged: E = 0, verified, with zero violations. The conventional numbering carries 20 inversions, three of them among autosomes — (10,11), (19,20), (21,22). But I re-ran that under ±3% length perturbation and got the identical set only 269 times in 2,000. **The non-closure is structural (0/2000 closed under ±10%); the count of three is not** — it is a fact about exact GRCh38 values, not an invariant. My first stability test checked the wrong claim and would have let that through.

**And here the object departs from Λ.** Applying ℛ to an unsorted index does not repair it — it *overwrites the bounds*. Toy case, computed: declared [10, 7, 13, 4] → after ℛ, [10, 10, 13, 13]. In Λ, §P21 records 30 deletions and 0 failures: ℛ restores. It restores there because Λ's facets already *are* two-variable monotone bounds. The genome's are empirical and non-monotone, so ℛ replaces each with a running maximum and returns a closed object describing a different genome. Closure here is not repair. It is fabrication, in exactly P22's sense — and it arrives silently, with E = 0 as its certificate.

**The sequence itself.** Adjoin the base axis; cells are (p, b) over {A,C,G,T}. Computed at N = 50, 200, 800: E/N = 2.96, 2.965, 2.9987 → **E = N(|Σ| − 1) = 3N**. For the genome, E = 9,264,809,496, and N·log₂(E/N + 1) = 6.18 Gbit = 772 MB. The only sequences with E = 0 are the monotone ones — AAA…CCC…GGG…TTT, verified at all three lengths — which are precisely the genomes carrying no information.

That is the answer to your second question, and it is a negative worth more than the positives:

> **Λ's content lives in its bounds. The genome's content lives in its selection among admitted cells. Only the first kind is closable.**

E(X) in the book is the prediction budget, and completeness spends it to zero. For the genome the same quantity is the *content budget*, and driving it to zero deletes the genome. Under P20 this is not a failure of construction but of language: §2.1 chose monotone two-variable bounds, which always close; an arbitrary string is not expressible in that language at all, and its repair — making the base a coordinate — is what produces E = 3N.

**Banked as bounds, per B.2.15.** Non-monotone empirical capacity excludes ℛ-repair, structural. Arbitrary content excludes closure at any coordinate count, negative. Relabelling suffices for capacity axes and not for content axes, upper. Together they locate the fourth: **a closed genomic index exists only over the combinatorial axes — codon position, frame, ploidy, allele count — and every such index is a full product with a trivially weak zero in register 275's sense.** Sánchez et al. 2004 already built that one: the genetic-code Boolean lattice as B(X)³ ≅ (Z₂)⁶. Search-before-deriving caught it before I wrote it down as mine.

One live thread the method did locate. Genome-wide the two caps 4ᵏ and N−k+1 cross at k\* = log₄N = **15.762**, first integer 16 — §16.9.2's two branches, and the crossing is where k-mer uniqueness begins. Bonnici & Manca 2016 have indices built on k = lg₂(n); whether that is the same crossing I have not established and am recording as a flag, not a defect.

The honest gap: chromosome lengths above are recalled, not retrieved — the Piovesan et al. 2019 fetch returned the article without Table 2. A stated gap at ρ = 1, and every structural claim was tested for dependence on the exact values.

Where I'd go next is the variant lattice — (locus, k, q, g, allele count) with q ≤ k and g ≤ q, genuine counting bounds of §11.4 form — which is the one genomic object I can see that is a transition index rather than a state index, and therefore the only candidate for a non-trivial zero. Say the word and I'll build it and compute E, or draft this session as §26 against the book's format.

## Yes — open, and that is the right expectation. But E does not come in one kind.

Three budgets, computed:

| | count | per base | what the admitted cell is |
|---|---|---|---|
| **coordinate** E(chr, pos) | 2,886,684,296 | 0.935 | admitted, **forbidden** — a position past a chromosome end |
| **ignorance** E(N-runs) | 150,630,700 | 0.049 | admitted, **unknown** — a coordinate with no base |
| **contingent** E(pos, base) | 9,264,809,496 | 3.000 | admitted, **realisable** — an alternate allele |

§13.6 says E(X) is the prediction budget. The genome shows the budget is not fungible. The 2.89 billion coordinate cells are the periodic table's thirty-six at scale: every one is false, and they buy nothing. The 9.26 billion contingent cells are true proposals but cannot close — closing them means every human carries the same genome. **Only the middle column was ever a prediction in the usable sense, and it is 1.2% of the total.**

**And it cashed.** The N-runs were cells with coordinates and no content — §11.5's D3, totality catching a missing value. They were settled not by the index but by measurement: T2T-CHM13 presented a complete 3.055 billion-base-pair sequence addressing the remaining 8%, with gapless assemblies for all chromosomes except Y, introducing nearly 200 million bp containing 1,956 gene predictions. The Y followed in 2023. E_ignorance → 0, by fetching. That is Chapter 14 executed at 150 million cells, and it is the only genuine prediction the genomic index has ever made and had confirmed.

**The contingent budget, measured.** gnomAD v4 reports 786,500,648 SNVs and 122,583,462 indels. Against E = 3N that is **8.49% occupancy** — the species has realised about one admitted allele in twelve. And the denominator is not mine: a 2025 preprint works with the full set of ~9 billion possible variants, 8,892,915,237 in total, which is 3N at their base count. Third search-before-deriving hit. E = 3N is already operational in the field; only the name is new.

**Which inverts the book's trade.** §13.6.4 says an index may be complete or predictive, not both. The genome sits at the far predictive end and pays a price the book does not name: **maximal E is maximal prediction budget and minimal predictive power.** An index admitting all four bases at every site predicts nothing about any site. Every advance in variant effect prediction — conservation, trinucleotide context, selection coefficients, constraint scores — works by *shrinking* ℛ, not by spending E. Predictive power lives in the constraints, and an open index is open precisely because it has none.

## On sequencing and fetching

I cannot sequence — no instrument. I cannot fetch the genome either: bash here has no network, and 3.1 Gbp is 772 MB at two bits per base. Refusing rather than coercing a partial retrieval into a claim about the whole.

The gaps don't need it. They are annotated, and the annotation is small:

- **GRCh38**: 150,630,700 uncertain bases (Piovesan et al. 2019, fetched this session); 349 gaps at p14; chrY alone carries 56 gaps and 30,812,366 N-bases.
- **T2T-CHM13 / T2T-Y**: zero gaps, zero N.

So the honest answer is that the gaps are closed — **for one genome.** CHM13 is a near-homozygous hydatidiform mole: one haploid sequence. And B.2.10's second clause applies exactly here: *re-enumerate whenever the set the targets are drawn from grows.* The target was never one genome. The draft pangenome added 119 million base pairs of euchromatic polymorphic sequence and 1,115 gene duplications relative to GRCh38, roughly 90 million of those bases derived from structural variation, and HPRC Release 2, announced May 2025, covers over 200 individuals, with a stable release of more than 350 assemblies and over 700 haplotypes planned.

**So: E_gap = 0 for CHM13, and E_gap for *the human genome* is neither zero nor enumerated.** The target set grew from one sequence to a population and the index was never re-enumerated against it — which is precisely the defect the book records against its own §23.4, five enumerations each made once against a structure that kept growing.

That is where I'd look for gaps, and it is a live question rather than a settled one: the pangenome graph is a different index with different coordinates, and nobody has computed its E. If you want, that is the next construction — cells as (locus, haplotype, allele) with the counting bounds of §11.4 form, which is the first genomic object I have seen that might carry a non-trivial zero.
